div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

A YOUNG man never thoroughly appreciates ' his own insignificance until he attends his own wedding. So far, the most notable example of men who "lived a double life " is afforded by the Siamese Twins.

"A LITTLE learning is a dangerous thing ; " but, for all that, the primary schools don't contain the dangerous classes. CHOIR TEACHER. -" Can you sing?" Lynx, flippantly—" Oh, I can take my chants with the rest."

" How do you distinguish an old fowl from a young one "By the t eth.'" Come, now, no joking; fowls have no teeth." "But I have." BEWARE of the men who smiles when he's angry; be is likely to he dangerous. And beware of the man who looks glum when he's glad ; he's probJ.bly a humourist.

"YES," said the primary Sunday schciol teacher, "the very hairs of our heads are numbered." And Tommy Bangs, jerking a blonde bristle out of his wicked little head, held it up and demanded— What number is that?"

A GREAT PITY.—Oid Freybeard : "It's a pity to keep such a pretty bird in a cage." Mrs. De Style : " it a shame? How perfectly ex- quisitely lovely it would look in a hat !" SOLD —Doctor:! "Clear case, Constant playing affected lungs. First symptoms of consumption. What is your instrument ? " Bandsman: " Drum

A ToucTuNG SIGHT.—A small boy investigating a newly-painted door. A COINCIDENCE.—Mrs. Janson said to Mrs. Lammis, in perfect cenfidence : "Do you know, mine is the prettiest baby in the word !" "Well, really now, what a coincidence !' said Mrs. Lam- mas. "So is mine ! " A SUNDAY-SCHOOL TEACHER complimented a little fellow one day for having behaved well in Sunday- school. "Yes," said the boy, "Pa said if I be- haved well in Sunday-school I need not go to church."

JACK PoTTER : What do you suppose becomes of all the counterfeit coins placed in circulation !" Rowne de Bout: "About evenly distributed be- tween the slot machines and the heathen." HEARTLESS DECEPTION.— Mr. Noopop : "My baby cries all night. I don't know what to do with it." Mr. Knowitt : "11l tell you what I did. As soon as our baby commenced to cry, I used to turn on all the gas. That fooled him. He thought it was broad daylight, and went to sleep. AN INNOCENT JOKER. —The man that makes a joke without intending it frequently amuses us more than the most ingenious of professional jokers. A milkman lately was charged with putting calves' brains in his milk. "Brains !" he exclaimed. "Why, I never had such a thing in my head?" A TRYING TIME. —Grigglo : "I hear you have a new lodger, Lettem—a musician. What instru- ment does he play?" Lettem (sadly) : "He dosen't play any instrument—he only tries to!" A SOLDIER upon the march found a horse-shoe, and stuck it in his belt, and as they were passing through a wood where some of the enemy lay in ambush, one of them fired, and the bullet by good fortune came right against the soldier's horse-shoe. " Aha 1' said he," "I can see that very little armour will serve a man's turn, if it is only put in the right place." GROCER (to five-year old miss) : "Well, what is it, little girl ?" Little Girl : " Mother sent me for a hall of string, an she wants it as strong as that butter you sold her yesterday." THE following doubtful compliment is a fragment from a love letter : "How I w;sh, my darling Adelaide, my engagements would permit me to leave town and come and see you. It would be like visiting some old ruin, hallowed by time, and fraught with a thousand pleasing recollections." A PERMANENT FENCE —Little Dick had been listening to the recitation in geography of an elder brother. "I know what an island is,' said he, to mamma. "Wll, what is it ? " asked mamma. "It's a little piece of land all fenced round with water," proudly answered Dick. His FIRST BRlEF.—First Young Barrister: "Allow me to con,6ra.tukte you. I saw you this morning hurrying along to the assize courts, with a brief-bag in your hand. So your first client has come ? " Second Ditto (with a leek of satisfaction) : "Yes, my tailor has taken out a summons against me ! " . .

AN Irish tenant farmer, returning from a some- what distant market late one afternoon missed his way, and got into a bog-hole, where he stuck fast. His landlord, who knew well the locality, chancing to pass shortly afterwards on horse back, noticed his tenant's dilemma, and smilingly shouted out— " Hallo, Pat! you ye got fixity of tenure now." "Yes, begorra !" ejaculated Pat, "and I'd be moightly obliged if yer honour wud evict me."

HOME THEATRICALS. - Little Ethel: "Oh, mamma, we is getting' up a be-utiful play! I is to be a statue, an' Johnny is to be a scluptor, an' he is to fall in love wiz me, an' then I am to come to life." Mamma: "And what are you to do after you come to life ?" Little Ethel : Guess 11l say 'Boo'!"
AN old miser slept for years with two thousand pounds under his mattress. It is not every one who can retire so often on a fortune. _ _

CHAMP: "Are you courting Miss Sterne now, Chumple ?" Chumple : 'No, she's courting me. She's commenced an action for nreach of promise of marriage against me !" THE POWER OF WEALTH. —Visitor: "Who is this Mrs. Bigmoney?" Resident: "She is our wealthiest woman.' Visitor: "Does she belong to your best families?" Resident: "Oh, no; they belong to her." FRIIND. —" Did you enjoy your sojourn in Europe?" Relic Hunter—" Enjoy it? I should say so! I cut some gold fringe from the Emperor's throne in Berlin, hooked a door-knob from the Vatican, broke an ear off an oh l statute in Italy, and chipped off a piere of Shakespeare's tomb. I wouldn't take a thousand dollars for 'em." CHIPPY : "My memory is failing me dreadfully, Sharpie." Sharpie : "I'm sorry to hear that, old man. By-the-by, could you lend me a ?' A SHOEMAKER hung out the following sign, and wondered what passers-by found so amusing: "Don't go elsewhere to be cheated. Walk in

here !" "WE must husband our resources," as the man said when he pocketed the two shillings his wife had earned for a day's washing. WAT-EP. DISAPPOINTMENT !—Fred (to Snobbing- ton, who has just returned from Venice) : "Well, my boy, how did you like Venice? Very fine— very pictutesque—eh Snobhington : "Oh, as to that, it was just my luck! Blest if they 'adn't 'ad a inundation, and all the streets was flooded !" MAGISTRATE (to "drunk and disorderly ") : "What are your means of support ?" Prisoner (facetiously) "Well, last night the policeman was. your worshin !"

The War Office is, I find, exhibiting some solici- tude that the younger soldiers shall not be over- exercised and over-trained. In an order just issued commanding officers are instructed to undertake shorter marches during the winter and to exercise discretion in excusing the younger soldiers from carrying their valises. They are also instructed to give greater care to the fitting of the men's boots, and are even told that in the evening during a march they should, wherever practicable, hold an inspection of the men's feet. This certainly is a new departure in military orders, and shows an unwonted solicitude at the headquarters for the younger soldiers.

I learn on very good authority that the Govern- ment do not intend to propose the House of Lords resolution until the eve of the dissolution, and this will be determined by the course of political events during the opening weeks of the session. The general opinion is, however, that the general elec- tion will take place before next harvest.

There is a rumour that Lord Rosebery has offered a baronetcy to Mr. Schnadhorst. No one will deny that the services of Mr. Schnadhorst to the Liberal cause merit recognition at the hands of the head of the Liberal party; but those who know what a singularly modest man the late chairman of the General Committee of the National Liberal Federa- tion is will not be at all suprised if he declines to accept any titular honour.

Mr. a J. Romanes, whose death about a year ago was so great a loss to speculative science, left be- hind him the manuscript of a book to which he had given the name of "Thoughts on Religious Problems." This work will soon be published, and will be look for with great interest by all evolu- tionists. The Rev, Charles Gore has undertaken to write a preface for the work, which is more likely to be critical or expository than biographical, since Mrs. Romanes herself is engaged on a life of her deceased husband. If Mr. Gladstone. Vilfjsecutes the intention with which he is at present credited, and writes a work on the early books of the Bible, that involve so many interesting problems in connection with the origin of civilisation. the primitive theo- logy, and the rise of the Jewish race and religion we shall this winter have three works all dealing with great religious problems from three widely different standpoints—the one by Mr. Gladstone just referred to, that by Mr. Romanes from the point of view of the Darwinian philosopher, and that by Mr. Balfour from the point of view of a speculative and metaphysical thinker.

The most interesting feature of the exhibition in commemoration of Gibbon, which opened on Mon- day at the British Museum, were the portraits of the great historian and his Bible. There were several portraits of him, and there were also very fine por- traits of his father and mother,to neither of whom, however, the historian bore the slightest resemb- lance. The two parents have rather pronounced noses, with the bridge disposed to be prominent. Everybody will remember from the engraved por- traits of Gibbon that his nose is gracefully scooped out at the place where the bridge was, and that it termintites in rather a substantial fleshy knob. One of Gibbon's portrait, quite as large as that taken of him by Sir Joshua Reynolds, was painted when he was 19 years of age, and it is remarkable that there it scarcely a feature of Gibbon at 19 which re,em- bles the Gibbon who sat to Sir Joshua. The lad's nose, like his father's and mother's, is full and pro- minent; and there is a slight disposition in the youthful mouth and chin to be full and fIP-hy, and a similar trait is discernible in his parents. This is the only feature, in fact, which the Gibbon of maturity retained from the Gibbon of 19. Sir Jogina's portrait of him is wonderfully brilliant and effective, and a copy of it which hangs by its side brings into striking prominence the master's power.

The election of Mr. Edward Evans, jun., as chair- man of the General Committee of the National Liberal Federation is regarded with the warmest approval by London Liberals. Men who have been in the North and known Mr. Evans's work are especially enthusiastic. It is some years since I first met him, and he has always given the impres- sion of a strong man and a brilliant organiser who can work hard.

It is believed—indeed it is known—that there are people who admire the modern bulldog. He is an amiable eccentricity who serves to show how extravagantly dog breeders can go wrong in the direction of fitness and right in the creation of deformity. A show got un by the South London Bulldog Society was opened on Tues- day at the Royal Aquarium. One of its features is a display of what are called "toy bulldogs.' A " toy " ought not to exceed 8113. in weight, and therefore it is wrong to give such a name to dogs more than double the weight. Some of the "toys" are genuine bulldogs who happen to be diminutive, and those imported from France are mere mongrels with something of the bulldog character about them, and yet with prick ears and other points which are abominable in the eyes of pedantic bulldog fanciers.

The conquering msrch of the Japanese army into China is not unlikely to have the most far-reaching effects on the future of the great empire which has contemptuously resisted for so long a period the influences of the civilization of the West. It has proved to China beyond doubt that the system of isolation amd stagnation on which she has been resting with so much placid confidence is unable to hold its own against a system inspired by the influences of European ideas; and it proves it in the best of all possible ways, by the trial of strength being between two Oriental people—one moved by the stimulus of a progressive life, and the other by its sluggish 'resistance to change. The present war may be the means of awakening the Chinese Government out of its lethargy, and of leading to the complete open- ing up of the country to modern civilisation. If it does not, China is hard to teach. It is now paying the penalty of its arrogant contempt for progress, and it will find the lesson costly both in prestige and money. At present the Chinese bubble is effec- tually pricked, and the money burden which the war will entail is as nothing to the humiliation the defeat of China by Japan involves. The true com- pensation would lie in the war arousing China from its long sleep. The German Emperor's song, both the words and the music of which boas', Imperial authorship. has at last been heard in this country, having been sung at Steinway Hall on Monday. It has all the advantages of Mr. Hayden Ciffin's fine vocalisa- tion, but the English audience was not under the obligation to subordinate art to loyalty, or truth to flunkeyism, and it expressed its judgment in the most reserved manner, and did not even call for an encore. In the competent hands of Mr. Professor Muller the translation of the song into English is as perfect as it could be made. It has no element in it which could appeal in the remotest degree to the heart or the sympathies of an Englishman. A thousand years ago the Scandinavian rovers might have clashed their shields and delivered a resounding " Hoch " over it after their draught of ale. It is difficult to conceive even a German delivering a " Hoch" over it. except as a mere tribute of admiration for his Emperor, for it is founded upon an utterly dead myth, and appeals to no genuine living human emotion, or to any true patriotic feeling like "Scots Wha Hae "or " Britons Never Shall be Slaves," or some of the modern Greek songs of independence. Yet the words have sub- stance in them and a splendid straightforward vigour which is much more characteristic of them than any poety they may be thought to contain. The melody is indifferent, and even below the quality of the words, and the words and the air alike will only survive the present as an Imperial curiosity. It is characteristic that w bile a new setting of the poor Scottish peasants' song of" Ca' the Yowes to the linowes" was cheered and encored to the echo by the saw audience, the song of the great Emperor produced scarcely a responsive* sound.

Throughout the whole of London the Free Churches are working with unbroken unanimity to secure a victory for the Progressive cause iu the ap- proaching School Board election. Not since the passing of Mr. Forster's Act has such interest been awakened among the Methodist electorate in this question. and the Wesleyan vote in Loudon bids fair to go solid for the Progressive party. ir 111 OXON'S NURSERY BOON

Mrs. Margaret Delan, the author of" John Ward, Prfadier," has written a new novel, which she entitles, "1 hilip and his Wife." The Queen of Sweden, who has always taken an inter- est in Swedish hospitals and the nursing of the sick, has had the first experiments made in Sweden with the new cure for diphtheria. The Crown Princess of Sweden does not, as was at one time feared, suffer from lung or throat affection, bu from ancemia. Whether she remains in Baden or goes to Southern Europe depends upon the weather. It is thought that the Princess of Wales will remain with her sister the Czarina until after the New Year. if not longer. The late Czar sent a message before his death asking her to come to Russia and stay for some time in order to c3mfort and console her sister. The Princess under the circumstances feels it to be her duty to fulfil the dying wishes of the Czar. The present Duchess of Sutherland owes her position to the superstition concerning the unluckiness of the number thirteen. One day at the house of the late Lord Rosalyn. it was discovered that there were thirteen per- sons at the dinner table. To add to this number Lady Millicent, a daughter of the house who had not yet come out, was sent for to join the party, and the young Marquis of Stafford was so charmed with her that he almost immediately after proposed wad was accepted. Nothing is s3ttlee for certain about the date of the Czar's marriage, but his formal betrothal to the Princess Alix makes the event of a foregone conclusion. In the Greek church the ceremony of betrothal if practically as binding as that of wedlock itself. Since her solemn reception into the Orthodox Communion, however, the Princess should be spoken of as Her Imperial Highness the Grand Duchess Alexandra Feodorovna. The change has certainly not made for simp icity in the matter of nomenclature, but ere long we hops to speak of her as the Czarina.
A Graceful House Gown.

For an elderly lady it may be said that a black gown I prettily made is always a suitable at-home dress, for whether it be black silk or black cashmere it can be arranged so that it will be becoming to the figure, and by the disposition of a little lace of some jet it can be made to have quite an elaborate air. So writes Isabel A. Mallon in the "Ladies riome Journal." As the close scrutiny is not given to a house dress that is to that one which is worn on the street, it is often possible to remodel a black gown, and by conAbining it with some other materials make it even more affective than it was originally. • A very dainty gown is an illustration of this. The back and sides are of black silk, which at one time formed a part of a dinner dress ; the front, which is just full enough to be graceful, is of soft,white China silk, its outline at each side being defined by a broad band of black passementerie, which, resting as it does against the white, has its design brought out, most effec- tively. The high collar, close to the throat, is of white ribbon, folded and fastened under a tiny rosette, but a flaring collar and revers of white lace are around the neck, and extending far over on the sleeves, then curve in to be made in soft jabots to the waste-line. The sleeves are of black silk, are extremely full, and stand out so that they form the foundations for that part of the lace collar that comes over them. At the wrist where they shape in, a tiny jabot of narrow white lace is arranged well on each outer edge. In effect a tea-gown is produced by this development of materials ; indeed, it may be said that it is almost one in reality.

ADDISON.

The little party, consisting of Giralda and Fay, Mrs. Pumpton and their shepherd guide, reached the little market town of Dalton within two hours after leaving Peggy Willsey's cottage, and without having encountered any hostile face. During the journey, necessarily slow, on account of the rugged roads, Giralda had thought much. Her determination to telegraph to her mother the joyful news of Fay's recovery had beenreconsidered. A telegram to the Lady Beatrice could not fail to attract the attention of Lord Hampton, and re- arouse his suspicions of something strange and con- cealed in his daughter's life. It were best, decided the young girl, to write to the fictitious address her mother had given her. The letter would be but a few hours in reaching the hands for which it was intended, and the brief delay would be of little consequence. As the travellers rode through the rudely paved streets of the little town, the clatter of their horses' hoofs brought the inhabitants to their doors, the arrival of strangers except on market days, being an event in this dull and sleepy little place. Suddenly Giralda utterred an exclamation, cheking her companion. She had seen upon the door-post of a brick dwelling the gilt sign of a" surgeon and physician." "Let us send the doctor to Peggy's before seek- ing lodgings," she said. "I cannot rest easy un- til I know the extent of Negwyn's injuries." Her proposition was acceded to. The party dis- mounted and entered the surgeon's office, finding its proprietor e. 12 home.... In a. few words Girald explained to him tliat- air accident had that morn- ing occurred on the Burnt Downs, ten miles away to the northward of Dalton, proceeding to explain the nature of the accident and her opinion oi the extent of N egwyn's injuries.

"I wish you to see the unfortunate man at once, sir," she said, in couclusion, with a gentle dignity that impressed the gray-haired, benevolent-looking surgeon. "It is most necessary to me that he should recover his reason, and I beg of you to spare no skill or pains in his behalf. I shall remain in Dalton for the present, and shall call daily for news of him. Be kind enough to go to him immediately. And finally," she added, drawing her purse, "let me pay you a retaining fee." She drew out and handed the surgeon a crisp ten-pound note, which he accepted, informing her that he should make all speed in attending upon his now patient at the Burnt Downs, and that he should exercise his best skill in Negwyn's behalf. "You said, I believe," he remarked, "that I should find him at the cottage of Peggy Willsey. I know that cottage well, and shall be within its walls in a little over an hour. I shall have news for you this evening of my patient, Miss." Gira Ida bowed, and arose, taking her depar- ture. "And now." she said, when they had all mounted and were riding along the street, "let us find our lodgings. .Jamie," and she turned to the shepherd lad, "Peggy told you the address of her friend to whose house we are going. Can you take us directly there ? " "We are almost the re now, Miss," rezlionded Jamie. " Here ! This is the place ! " He halted befoce a small pastry-cook's shop, and I dismounted. Giralda handed Fay to him, and then also dismounted.

"This the place I" said Mrs. Pumpton, with a sweeping glance at the building and the neigh- boring ones. "What a refuge for a Trevelyan !" She resolutely repressed a groan as she alighted on the horse-block with some difficulty. The pastry-cook's shop occupied the lower floor of a neat brick house two stories in height. It was surrounded by shops, being in the business portion of the place, but it had a distinguishing air of neat- ness which the keen eyes of the Park hcwAckeeper were not slow to discover. Jamie led the way into the shop. There was neither shopkeeper nor customer within. Mrs. Pumpton bestowed a critical glance upon the white loaves, braided and twisted and plain, which loaded the counter, and upon the crisp tarts and cakes which filled the neat show- case. "I am hungry, Giralda," whispered Fay, quite overcome by the pleasant odors. At this moment the door of an inner room opened, and a pleasant-faced, middle-aged woman, of business aspect, entered the shop, passing briskly behind the counter. , "This is Mrs. Jones," said Jamie, by way of ' introduction. Giralda briefly explained to the shopwoman that she had been rec ommended by Peggy Willsey, of the Burnt Downs, to apply to her friend Mrs. Jones, at Dalton, for quiet lodgings. Mrs. Jones, who was a genuine Welshwoman, unlike Mrs. Pum pton, who was English, smiled all over her broad face in hospitable welcome.

"Any friend, whether lofty or lowly, of Peggy Willsey is sure of the best at my command," she said, in a broken accent, which seemed to utterly fascinate poor little tired Fay. "And, as it hap- pens, my first floor is vacant. Will Miss be pleased to walk up and look at it ? " Giralda assented, and Mrs. Jones led the way into a neat back parlour, which opened upon a little garden, and thence' by a fight of stairs, to the second floor. Fay kept at his sister's side, manfully tugging her little travelling bag, of which he deemed it his duty to relieve her, and Mrs. Pumpton toiled after them. The second floor consisted of two rooms, con- nected by a door. The front room was furnished as a drawing-room, with a spider-legged table, an antiquated nofa, and the inevitable lodging-house cheffonier, with its display of old cracked china of every kind, colour and manufacture. Two faded, dauby portraits in oil of Mrs. Jones's las parents adorned the walls. The windows were provided with green shutter blinds, to be elevated or lowered at pleasure. The back room looked out upon the garden, and was simply furnished as a bedroom. The neatness pervading both rooms was perfect, and gave to them a charm they would otherwise have lacked. Giralda promptly decided to take the rooms, settled upon terms, to include board to be served In her own parlour, and paid the first week in advance. And then with a sense of relief, she sat down, drawing Fay to her side. Mrs. Pumpton seated herself by the window. Jamie, who had attended them up stairs, now bashfully made known the fact that he must re- turn immediately to the Burnt Downs, Peggy and the sheep, and took his leave, greatly delighted with the handsome gratuity Giralda bestowed upon him at parting. 'We have had a hard journey since leaving Trevelyan Park, Mrs. Pumpton," said the young girl, as she unpacked her bag for writing materials. "You must remain here to-night and get well rested before going home." "I don't like to leave you at all, Miss," said the housekeeper, Fighin 2:. "If it wasn't that I love in 7 lord in spite of all his faults, 1 would stay with you, and not even think of going back. But if he were to make himself sick with his rage, or get himself into a stroke of apoplexy, no one could take care of him as I could." "Yes, you must go back to-morrow. Poor uncle! I love him, although he hates me, Mrs. Pumpton. It is very hard to feel that he believes me what Lord Adlowe said, false and scheming and treacherous." 'rue tears gathered in Giralda's eyes, and a bitter pang rent her heart at the thought that her uncle's love for her had turned to hatred. If she had only known that at that moment, con- quering his pride, he was wildly grieving for her, his soul convulsed with anguish and fear lest he had lost her forever I Giralda wrote a guarded letter, announcing, Fay's safety under her own guardianship, and giv- ing her present address, declaring that she should remain where she was until she should learn her mother's wishes. The missive was addressed as the Lady Beatrice had directed. A second letter was then written, addressed to Lord Crosvenor. It was not a love letter, in the usual acceptation of the term. In the most modest and delicate manner, Giralda told his lordship of the cause of her flight from the Park, gave him her present address, and assured him of her present sect., ity The letters finished she went out and posted them herself. She came back quite bright and hopeful. " Now I have nethitig to do but to wait, l',lrs. ill,trepto:e" she t-ai.id. " I shall hear from mamma, by tile day alter to-morrow. div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MT DEAREST NELLIE,

Fur promises to be very fashionable this season. lb is no longer fashioned into the loose, straight garments of old, but modelled on all the latest designs, in the shape of short, tight Eton bodices, long, loose-fitting coats, three-quarter coats, both tight and semi-fitting, and the orthodox loose cape. Sable, seal, skunk, beaver, bear, chinchilla, fox, Thibet, Persian lamb, and mink are among the favoured varieties, while squirrel and ermine are used as linings. Velveteen is now trimmed with the rather uncommon combination of fur, the latter being used as borders on the skirt and to the collar and wrists, while a deep vandyked lace collar gives a touch of brightness to the whole. A smart little bonnet, suitable for present wear, has a point back and front, and is square at each side. It is composed of nasturtium-red velvet, and the trimmings consist of rosettes of black satin ribbon, jet osprey, and plume of bleak feathers, with a large loop bow of black satin ribbon at the back. Narrow strings of satin ribbon are tied in a bow under the chin. A good deal of the new plait made of satin cord and chenille is now being used, especially in the charming colour which sometimes goes by the name of "petunia," but is the exact tone of ' damson juice. Tokes are the dominant mode, and an exquisite one I have just seen is of the new chenille passementerie.

The shape of fashionable jackets is varied. They may be worn shorter than for some time past, or at the usual three-quarter length. The double- breasted reefer shape is popular, and is chiefly fashioned in rough, dark serge, with skirt to cor- respond. For very cold days, the sable throatlet supplies the necessary warmth round the neck. There is, however, a greb:t sameness when everyone you meet wears either a tight•fitting or loose. fronted jacket, all with the same full sleeves, and the same arrangement at the throat. A very sty- lish garment is the York over jacket of thick grey Oxford chevoit, with velvet collar and cuffs.

The new corset vest, as it is called, is made high to the throat, and fastens with gilt buttons. Very smart ones are shown in red cloth, which go well with dark blue costumes. Some have fancy spots in coloured silks woven into them, and others are of velveteen shot in two or three colours. Although the long basques have gone out, some tailor-made costumes have long coats, graduated away from hips, with which a contrasting waistcoat is worn. One I noticed in brown cloth had a crocodile leather vest, and the edge of shirt was bordered the same. A stylish girl's coat in fawn box•oloth looked well with fawn felt hat, trimmed with emerald green velvet.

Black woollen crapon is still a favourite material; some of the new designs—waved, crinkled, and silk-striped—are very pretty as well as inexpen- sive. For best wear, a becoming style is to have the skirt and sleeves of orepon, with a coloured satin bodice, covered in black chiffon. It is nob necessary to invest in a good satin, as one of ordinary quality is equally effective as an expens- ive make, provided the colour is bright. Striped grenadine is also suitable for the purpose, and is more durable. Bright grass-green under black Is very pretty. And now a word as to needlework. Felt work still holds its own, and the newest kind has the ground striped in various soft shades with excellent effect. Quaint egg-cosies in felt are in the shape of pheasants sitting on nests, while the most recent Introduction in teapot cosies is a reproduction of the pot itself in felt, with satin handle and spout,. It is, however, decidedly more odd than pretty. Among minor needlework novelties I may mention the bulrush pin-cushions made of brown plush and green satin, the little bag purses tatted in coloured cotton and finished with gilt mounts (these sell well at bazaars), and the moulded paper initial letters which are intended to be tacked on hand- kerchiefs, pillow-cases, &c. 9 and then sewn over with embroidery cotton. The letters are well designed and inexpensive, and with their aid the most complete novice can scarcely fail to be successful in working initials. Yours lovingly, JRNNne.

div.head: EXTRAORDINA ;-Y SCENE IN A THEATRE.
div.p: EXTRAORDINA ;-Y SCENE IN A THEATRE.
A JEALOUS WIFE AND HER GALLIVANTING HUSBAND.

An exciting incident was witnessed in the Prince's Theatre, Blackburn, at ten o'clock $4 n Saturday night. A gentleman well known in Manchester cotton circles was seated in the stalls with two ladies, when a thini lady, said to be his wife, rushed down the gangway and attacked him from the rear. ,belabouring him on the head with an umbrella, and crying" Come out of that, sir." The gentleman, amid a roar of amusement, bolted from the theatre, with his wife in hot pursuit. She caught him again outside, but the policeman on duty detained her until the husband had got away.

div.head: QUEER FOODS,
div.p: QUEER FOODS,

The Arabs and the Frenchmen appear to relish horse flesh. In Paris alone there are ag many as 150 butchers who deal in that sort of meat exclusively, and 20,000 horses were consumed last year. But the French are cnail-eaters also. The monthly consumption of snails in Paiis was recently estimated by the million, and there are at least 100 restuarants, and 3,000 private tables, at which customers consume these appetising. morsels. The sale is so large that 100,000 lb. weight of snails are sold daily in the Paris market for food ; and 2,000 tons of snails are eaten yearly in that one city.

_ The Cing,alese USA the bee as an article Of food, chew- ; log up the insect after they have extracted all the hor ey. The taste of the Hindus are in some sense refined. Great care is bestowed on the cultivation of the water-lily in many parts of India, and the flowers are used for food. The fruit of some species, especially those that grow in the neighbourhood of the lakes of Cashmere, is rich in starch, and pleasant to the palate, haying much the same flavour as the chesnut. R,aseleaf jam is a com- mon article of food in Roumania, where roses are grown in enormous quantities for that purpose. There are queer facts concerning the eating and drink- ing of the Chinese. The edible does of China are greatly relished. They are known by their bluish-black tongues. These quiet creatures, which never bark, are killed in r_•re.a numbers, the estimate being about 4,500,000 yearly. Then the Celestials are fond of a soup made of edible birds'-nests—the homes of a small swallow, com- posed of a gum-like substance,not unlike isinglass. Each I nest is about as large as a goose's egg and as thick as a spoon, weiehing from a quarter to halt an ounce. Con- sidering that the Chinese will buy them for nearly ' twice their weight in silver, it is not to he wondered at that Siam exported no less than six and a half tons of these nests last year to Hong Kong. The Japanese are extremely creel in their cooking. They cut every atom of flesh off a living fish piecemeal. Then in the same part of the world we find the people of Cochin China preferring rotten eggs to fresh ones. In India the fond seems equally repulsive, for the pariahs of that country are not above a struggle with the dogs and vultures for putrid carrion. The New Caledonians, so travellers tell us, are passion- ately fond of roast spiders, and hunt up these creatures with great eagerness. The Samoans dearly love the worm, and esteem it the greatest delicacy obtainable. They are not the worms of our own country, but" thick, juicy fellows, of various colours." In South America the savage tribes will swallow anything that is eatable. devouring serpents, lizards, and centipedes. Others in the West Indies esteem as a great luxury a large cater- pillar found upon the palm trees. Use goes a long way to disabuse one's mind of prejudice. That nsust be so, for some people like clay. In the most remote parts of Fweden and in Finland a kind of earth is occasionally mixed with bread; but we must remember that this earth contains infusoria. Earth-eaters are found in all countries of the torrid zone. In cold climates the people eat their food uncooked, but intensely frozen. The natives of South Greenland prepare themselves for a long journey in the cold by a course of frozen seal. In winter they bury a whole seal in the snow. The flesh, half frozen,half putrid, is eaten with a keen appetite. The Alaskans are great believers in hotch-potch. Whatever is eatable goes into the pot—herries, musk- rat, seal meat, fresh and stale salmon,grease,goat,sheep, and bear. When it is properly cooked,the whole village joins in the feast, each person helping himself with his hands.

My flight from the Park when he called this morning and I think he did not go back to London. I shall soon be well guarded. And until then I shall be quite safe with good Mrs. Jones." "Where are the horses ?" asked Fay, looking down into the street from the window. _

"In Mrs. Jones's stable, dear, with the donkeys that draw her baker's cart," answered Giralda,, smiling. "They are well cared for." Mrs. Pumpton declared that she did not know whether to return to the Park or remain with Giralda, and in the midst of her indecision Mrs. Jones came up to clear the spider-legged table in readiness for supper. "Those servants have got it all their own way at the Park," groaned Mrs. Pumpton, in the in- tervals afforded by the hostess's frequent trips below. "No one to see to them, and as sure as I'm a living woman, I've left the key of the store- room in the lock, and all the tea and coffee and sugar and candles at the mercy of them crea- tures. I must go back. There's no two ways about it. The balance was turned. The question was de- cided beyond further doubt. The table soon creaked under the tempting sup- per displayed upon it by Mr.s Jones, who had been somewhat enlightened in regard to Giralda's identity by the Park housekeeper, and who was secretly determined to be worthy the honour of sheltering and boarding two members of the "real quality," as she termed Giralda and Fay. After supper, when night had fallen, Giralda put Fay to bed, and soon after attended by Mrs. Pumpton, walked to the surgeon's for news of Negwyn. "He is not dead, Doctor ? " "No, not by a good deal 1" responded the doc- tor, cheerfully, evidently at a loss to comprehend the interest of the young lady in his new patient. "He has had a hard experience, Miss. Few men could have gone through it even so well as he. He is raving with fever now " "Can the fever not be broken up ? " asked Gir- alda.

"It will have to run its course Miss. It has full hold upon him. He has a good constitution, and we must hope for the best. I will attend him regularly, and use my best skill in his be- half ! " Giralda was silent a moment. Then she asked, in a low voice:

"What do you think of his case, Doctor ? " The physician studied her pale face an instant, as if to calculate the effect of his reply, and then answered: "Besides the fever, his leg is fractured. It's a bad case, Miss ; and, to be perfectly frank with you, I think it's an even chance between life and death ! "

A low moan arose to Giralda's lips. She reso- lutely repressed its utterance, and looked at the doctor with a yet paler 'face and dilating eyes. "If he should die," she said, in a half-whis- per, "do you think he would have his senses first ? "

"It is possible," replied the doctor, compassiona- ting her evident distressful anxiety. "I cannot deceive you, Miss. He may sink into a stupor and never awaken, never know any one. And, again, he may recover. I have known recoveries from just such desperate cases. We may consider it, as I said before, an even chance." "Then I will hope !" said the maiden. "That man, Doctor, holds a secret in his keeping which I would give worlds to have him declare to the world! I will go to Peggy's cottage at any time when you think the crisis is near. And until then I will call or send daily for tidings. You will visit him daily ? " The doctor assented, remarking that the season was healthy and he had few patients to visit, and censequently could and would devote mueh time to unfortunate Negwyn. Giralda thanked him and withdrew, returning wit'n Mrs. Pumpton to her lodgings. They separated at an early hour, retiring to their beds. Giralda long lay awake, with Fay nestled in her arms, her thoughts at one moment with her father and Rupert in their unknown retreat, the next with the Lady Beatrice at Hampton House, where a gay mask concealed her ladyship's break- ing heart; again, with Lord Trevelyan at the Park picturing him as she had last seen him, magnificent in his rage and scorn; and then reverting to poor Negwyn, whose possible confession could turn all this darkness into light, all this sadness into joy. "Oh, that he may live to clear poor papa's name!" she murmured, again and again. With this prayer on her lips, she fell asleep at last, and did not awaken until the morning.
She sprang up the moment of awakening, and made her toilet before she aroused Fay, whose slumbers were unusually late. Having dressed him, she went into the parlour, where Mrs. Pump- ton awaited her.

"I must be on my way very soon, Miss Giralda," said the worthy woman, sadly. "I've a long ride before.me. It goes hard to leave you here among strangers, but your sweet face makes friends for you anywhere. Mrs. Jones told me she'd do anything for you." Giralda soothed the housekeeper, protesting that she did not at all dislike being left to herself, and Mrs. Pumpton, under these kindly assurances, recovered her usual cheerfulness and appetite, so that when breakfast was brought in she was herself again. The meal over, she took an affecting leave, and went down stairs. Giralda and Fay, from their windows, watched her mount, and ride slowly and alone down the street.

At the nearest corner the worthy soul halted, and waved an affectionate farewell, her eyes full of tears, and then she touched up the stout cob, who ambled gayly along, much to tile delight of the urchins along the street. At the further end of the straggling street which composed the town—at a point where there were fewer houses, and these were set in larger gardens —Mrs. Pumpton beheld a hwseman approaching swiftly, entering the place. With an instinctive desire to look her best, she composed her agitated face, and brushed her baud across her tear-blinded eyes. At the same moment, seeing the horseman fully, she uttered a cry of wild dismay. The horseman was Lord Adlowe. He recognised her at the same moment, and urged his horse forward in quick bounds, while Mrs. Pumpton looked around her with some vague, wild hope of escape. He came up to her before she had time to de- cide, in her bewilderment, upon a course of action. His face, full of sinister meaning, lighted up with a savage glow, and his eyes gleamed jubilantly as he leaned forward and dexterously caught her bridle.

"Good morning, Mrs. Pumpton," he exclaimed, mockingly. "We are well met! This is like my old luck, meeting you at the very moment when I was thinking of you and longing for the sight of your pleasant old face." Mrs. Pumpton strove in vain to reply. She could not command her voice to speak. "Alone, eh ? " continued Adlowe, gayly. "And bound for Trevelyan Park, of course 1 That is well. My lordly uncle is distressed at your ab- sence, my worthy Pumpton. He thinks you have deserted him. Charming place, this DJ- ton! '
"Let go my bridle, my lord!" ejaculated the housekeeper, in a fury. Let go, I say! If you don:t I'll scream 1 I'll strike you. I'll raise a _ ..
crowd ! "

Lord. Adlowe arched his brows curiously, and looked at her as if she had been a natural curi- osity. " What spirit ! " he ejaculated, in seeming aston- ishment. " And at her time of life! Who would have believed that so much coltishness lingered in this venerable creature." "One word, Pumpton, and name your own re- ward. Did she take the train ?" "Find out for yourself," cried ~he woman. "There's your word, and all the reward I ask is for you to get out of my way." "Be careful ! Be careful !" hissed the refigate lord. "It is not safe to auger me. You know me of old, Dame Pumpton. fwarn you lam a des- perate man. Where is that girl? " "If you wait till I tell you, you'll be a pretty old man, that's all !" declared the housekeeper, plucking up spirit. " Miss Giralda is with friends. Her mother and Lord Grosvenor have been written to—"

"She is in Dalton then?" interrupted his lord- ship. eagerly. "I didn't say so. Dalton is a railway station. It is possible for Miss Giralda to have reached The Evergreens since yesterday." This mocking speech, and his lordship's mocking manner, caused Mrs. Pumpton to actually choke with passion. "Keep cool I" advised Lord Adlowe. "I should dislike to be detained as a u itness at a coroner's inciu,st in the present state of aftair.t. Where aid yon leave Miss Giralcia? " sirs. Pumpton glared at him without 'replying. he b said Acllowes

"Well, I shall easily find her. I know you must just have left her. I have traced you from the Park, my good woman. 1 understand all about he rescue of the boy, and that he is with his sister. t shepherd lad, who I met and deftly questioned, told me that, and also that Peggy Wilisey is too busy with the care of a dying friend to be longer trustworthy. I have not been to the Downs cottage myself, the meeting with the shepherd having apprised me folly of what I most wanted to know."
"Then most likely, you know where Miss Gir- alda is," said the housekeeper, with a ghastly amile.

"Not so. My gentle shepherd grew suspicious when I asked him the question, and flatly declined to answer it. I offered him money but he was insensible to its charms. He said the lady had trusted him and spoken kindly to him, and he would not betray her. You see the superiority of beauty over mere lucre. But you, my good Pumpton, will not refuse me your confidence, I feel assured."
There was a deadly glitter in his eyes before which the woman secretly quailed in sickening fear, but she looked up at him defiantly, and an- swered:

"You think, my lord, that I am less faithful than a shepherd lad. You don't know me. Let me pass." "But did she go on the train? Did she go back to the Park, or to the Evergreens? You shall an- swer me, old woman. By heaven! I will loosen your tongue for you." He caught at her bridle more closely as the horse pranced a little. Mrs. Pumpton was a woman of spirit. Her eyes flashed angrily at her persecutor. "Hands off, my lord ! " she cried.

He laughed, and drew nearer. With a quick, unexpected movement, the Park housekeeper snatched up her little riding whip, and brought it down with all her force upon the white jewelled hand of her enemy. With an oath and a cry of pain, Adlowe invol- untarily withdrew his blood-marked hand, and his horse backed a few steps in affright. "Let them teach you how to treat respectable, honest women, my Lord Adlowe," said Mrs. Pumpton, triumphantly. "Now do your worst. We'll see which will win."

She touched up her cob, and rode swiftly on her course, not deeming it best to return to Giralda, lest by doing so she should bring upon the maiden the discovery she desired to avoid. "I can't do better than go to the Park," she thought. "Miss Giralda is among friends, and that villain won't dare touch her, even if he finds her. And to-morrow Lord Grosvenor will be with her to protect her. She is surely safe." Thus stifling her misgivings, Mrs. Pumpton continued her journey. Lord Adlo we, on his prancing, curveting steed, looked after her with a scowl of hatred.

"I'll find that girl, if I have to search every house in Dalton," he muttered. "First to the railway stations. Then to inquire of the street urchins and idlers if such a young lady has been seen here. Curse it all! she's made me enough trouble. She has yet to find that obstacles in my way are only so many incentives to pursuit. Ah I lam very near to you, Giralda Trevelyan. I shall soon have you in my power, never again to lose you." He wrapped up his disfigured hand in his pocket- handkerchief, and, full of vengeful passions, rode slowly into the town, sending vigilant glances on every side and at every window in the hope of catching sight of Giralda's face.

THERE is something solemn in the tones of a great bell striking midnight, especially if you are a mile from home, and know that your wife is sitting behind the hall door waiting for you.

"Do birds think ?" asks a writer, in opening an article. If they do, we should like to know what a canary bird thinks of a woman who stands up in a chair and talks baby talk through the brass wires of the cage. 'I NEVER saw such a woman in all my life," said Bess; 'you are never satisfied with anything." "People who knew the man I took for a husband," replied Mrs. 8., "think, on the contrary, that I am very easily catir,fied." A contempo- rary is grieved to learn that his "brother of the quill has a wife with one eye." "No," said an old lady, "I'm not one to talk agin my neighbours, or say anything behind their backs. Now, there is Mrs. Brown, she who lives over in the corner house. I may not like her very well, still there's no reason why I should run her down. But Ido feel miserably sorry for poor Mr. Brown and the children."

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDLANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDLANS.

Mr. John Mclntyre presided over the fornightly meeting of the Board which was held oil Tuesday in the Workhouse, Dutton. There were also present —The Rev-. J. W. Tanner and Dr. Gastahli, Messrs. Joseph Knowles (vice-chairman), S. Taylor, J.P., T. Handley, J.P., T. Baxter, C.C., S. Yarwoon, A. R. Norman, T. Lea, J. Stokes, E. Bratherton, J. L. Jones, John Weir, Edward Aaron, Thomis Lewis, H. E. Heywood, J. Brandreth, J. NI. Williams, W. Turner, C. W. Davenport, G. Priestner„l. W. Baguley, C. Mounfield, C. T. Whitley, John Ashton (Clerk), and George Ashton (deputy-cle: k). A SCHOOLMASTER WANTED.

The Clerk stated that only two applicatiens had been received for the post of workhouse schoolmaster one applicant was unsuitable, and the other had withdrawn owing to the small salary. APPLICATION FOR AN INCREASE OF SALARY. A letter, asking for an increase ot salary, wa.4 received from Mr. W. R. de Prez,relieving officer of the Bud worth district. Since his appointment, at the present salary of £75, his duties had materially increased, ana he was compelled to use a pony and trap in order to get through his work. The cost of out relief had been gralually re- duced, since he held the position, by over one-third per annum, and this without any attendant hardship to any case of genuine destitution. Through his holding the positions of registrar of births and death, and vaccina- tion officer, a saving to the union had been effected of from £7 to £B.—Several members of the Board spoke highly of Mr. de Prez's capabilities and thought tbat he was deserving of an advance. Eventuilly the matter was referred to a small committee to deal with.

LETTER OF THANKS. The Clerk reporte that a letter had been received from Mr. John Whitlow, of Tannery Farm, Preston Brook, thanking the Board for their kind sympathy in the sad bereavement the family had Bust tined.

COUNTY RATES. The Cleik of the Peace in a letter to the Board stated that the County Council had ordered that the folkwing rates be levied for the half-year ending 31st March next :—County rate, 3d. in the £ ; general police rats, Id. in the £ ; and local police rates for the Runcorn Union it in the £. These were the same as in the cor- responding period last year.

ASSESSMENT CCIMAILL 114,E. The Chairman said that the above committee had met that morning, and they had considered it a wise course to engage a professional valuer to assess the 'works of Messrs. E. Timmins and Sons, Limited,of Run- corn. Before doing sothowever,the committee required the Board's sanction.—Mr. Knowles gave notice of his intention at the next meeting of the Board, to move that the request of the committee be acceded to.

div.head: FINANCE
div.p: FINANCE

Mr. Brandreth reported on behalf of the Finance Committee that the balance in the treasurer's hands amounted to £1,650 19s. The amount of arcounts re- quired for payment was £166 3s. Bcl., which included the following sums for relief :—Runcorn, £B5 ; Prods- ham, £3O; Budworth, £l9.

div.head: AFFAIRS OF THE IRISH PARTY.
div.p: THE AFFAIRS OF THE IRISH PARTY.
PLAIN SPEAKING BY MR. MTARTHY.

An important private meeting of the Irish Parliamen- tary party was held in Dublin on Monday, Mr. Justin M`Carthy presiding. Mr. M`Carthy, in opening the proceedings, announced that the Paris funds had been released, and would be administered in accordance with a previous decision of the party. He then proceeded to refer to the incident of Mr. Gladstone's cheque. He briefly explained that he had accepted the cheques from Mr. Gladstone and Lord Tweedmouth not knowing that they were not offered spontaneously, but were in reply to a circular. The issue of that circular was, he said, the blunder of a clerk, and the Committee ot the party were free from responsibility for or knowledge of its issue. "But the real and the supreme and the only point," continued Mr. M'Carthy, "which we and the country regard as worthy of serious consideration is whether such matters are to be made the subject of public discussion. Deliberately, emphatically, know- ing the full responsibility of the words I use, I have to declare to you that the continuance of these public disputes is incompatible with the safety of our movement. They have lowered our prestige, our influence, and our efficiency as a Parlia- mentary force, have given joy to our enemies, have saddened and disheartened our people at home and abroad,and have on more than one occasion, brought the party and the whole movement to the very verge of financial bankruptcy. The question is not one between individuals; the one issue is between unity and dis- ruption, between the preservation and the destruction of the party." Mr. M`Carthy, in conclusion, asked that his statement should be handed to the press, and said that the responsibility for a continuance of the present state of things would now rest, not on him but on the party, who must either endorse or reject his views. A resolution approving of the Chairman's statement and authorising its publication was met by an amendment declaring that its publication was only calculated to prolong controversy, and that the protest against the acceptance of Ministerial subsidies was called for in the circumstances ; and that they should now pass to the next business. The amendment was defeated 'by 38 votes to 14. Other resolutions dealt with the alliance with the Liberal party, the abolition of the House of Lords yeto, and the land question.
RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

On Tuesday afternoon the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority was held in the Boardroom of the Dutton Workhouse, Mr. John Mclntyre occupying the chair. There were also present the Rey. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. C. T. Whitley, J. Brandreth, H. E. Heywood, J. M. Williams, J. Stokes, J. Knowles, J. Weir, E Aaron, T. Lewis, T. Baxter, C.C., W. Turner, C. W. Daven- port, J. L. Jones, G. Priestner, C. Mounfield, E. Bratherton, J. W. Baguley, John Ashton, clerk; J. Ashton' deputy clerk; J. Farringtnn, nuisance in- Spector; and Dr. Adams, medical off-Tr ot health.

div.head: ACCOMMODATION FOR COWS.
div.p: THE ACCOMMODATION FOR COWS.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board relative to the regulations proposed to he adopted by the Authority respecting the Dairies, Cowsheds, and Milkshops Order of 1885. The letter stated that if the Sanitary Authority decided to require only 450 cubic feet of free air space for each cow, they would rot raise any further objection ; hut it must be clearly understood that the pntire responsibility for so doing would rest with the authority. They should proceed with the adoption of the regulations as already explained.—On the proposition of Mr. Williams it was decided to proceed in the ordinary way.

div.head: MR: FARRINGTON AND THE SI7RVEYORCHTP.
div.p: MR: FARRINGTON AND THE SI7RVEYORCHTP.

A letter was received from the Local Government Board referring to tho ro-a.ppointmcnt of Mr. J. Farring- ton as nuisance inspector and surveyor, in which no salary had been assigned to him for the latter position. The Board informed the authority that it was obvious under such an arrangement that the salary assigned to the office of inspector of nuisances would in fact cover re- muneration for the performance of the important duties 2S surveyor under the urban powers with which the Authority had been vested. As, however, repayment from the county fund was made in respect of the salaries of inspector of nuisances, but was not made in respect ot remuneration for performance of surveyor's duties, it was imperative that the payment for the two classes of services should be kept distinct. Under those circum- stances the Board must request that the Sanitary Autho- rity would give the matter their further consideration.— Alter some discussion it was resolved that the matter be deferred until the formation of the Wstrict Council.

THE AUTHORITY AND THE COUNTY COUNCIL. Mr. Fa.rrineton' nuisance inspector, submitted a report on the analysis of water recently brought before the Health Committee of the Cheshire County Council, and on which they had passed a resolution. He dealt with each case in detail, and brought forth facts which proved that the Authority had not been backward in discharg- ing their duty in dealing with impure water as had been stated at a recent meeting of the Health Committee of the County Council. The fact that the Authority had submitted the large number of 350 samples of water for analysis was in itself conclusive evidence that great attention had been ,eiven to the matter. Instead of the Authority being defaulters they had been the harbingers and aggressors. as the Authority had been the first to put into force the provisions contained in the Public Health (Water) Act, 1878. As an officer (of the Authority he (Mr. Farrington) claimed to being partly instru- mental in bringing about the present economical arrangement with the City Analyst for analysing waters, as well as some credit to himself for other matters. He thought. it would only he fair to the Authority and its officers that a copy of the report should be forwarded to the County Medical officer of Health.— On the proposi- tion of Mr. Heywood, scconded by Mr. Weir, it was decided to forward a copy of the report to the County Medical Officer. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. Adams, medical officer to the Authority, reported that a fresh case of scarlet fever had occurred at Rock Savage, Clifton, and one of diphtheria at Frodsham. The house where the last patient resided, had recently had the new water supely laid on to it. Strong com- plaints had been made of the emanations from the main sewer opposite the house, which at times were very offensive, and might probably be held accountable for the disease. Three fresh cases of scarlet fever had occurred at Weston Point. On investigation, one of these cases appeared to he very doubtful. A case of typheid fever had also broken out at Weston Peint, the cause of it being very obscure. There was, however,an entrapped grid in the back yard. Milk was sold on the premises, and arrangements had been made for the milk and dairy utensils to be dealt with outside the premises altogether, during the isivaipa uan e of the disease. After a temporary lull, scarleefeVer had broken nut afresh in Kingsley and had invaded the Boys Home. There Were in all ten cases in the towrship, of which number one had terminated fatally. One case of diphtheria had also occurred. With reference to the Boys' Home, the cases were isolated as far

as the arrangements of the Home would permit ; two ' nurses had been obtained ; whilst all the boys were being kept from school. In consequence of the increas- ing spread of the disease, the medical officer recom- mended that all the schools in Kingsley be closed for at least a month, and that their re-opening be considered again at the end of that time, in cannection with the extension or decline of the epidemic no fresh cases had been reported from Norley. 'I hat (Tuesday) morning he had received a complaint of the insanitary condition of six cottages in Kingsley, which required immediate attention.—The report was approved of and adopted.

div.head: SMALLPDX HOSPITAL.
div.p: THE SMALLPDX HOSPITAL.

Mr. Williams stated that he had recently visited Man ehester and had called at the offices of Mr. Dunlop, the land agent to the Manchester Ship Canal Company. As that gentleman was not to be seen, Mr. Wallace was interviewed on the subject of retaining the hospital at Moore for the use of the Sanitary Authority. Mr. Wallace told him that no arrangements had been made with Sir Richard Brooke to let the hespital to him but that they had been waiting to hear what the Authority intended doing —whether they required to retain the hospital for a further term or not. Sir R. Brook had made the Com- pany an offer to take the hospital for the purposes of one of his gamekeepers, and also to lodge cattle there. They were quite willing to allow the Authority to retain the hospital on condition that they paid the same sum in rent as was offered by Sir Richard Brooke, viz., £2O per annum. He (Mr. Williams) would like to give notice that at the next meeting he would move that those terms be accepted and that the hospital be retained for another twelve months.

div.head: STORY OF OLIVER WENDELL HOLMES.
div.p: A STORY OF OLIVER WENDELL HOLMES.

A London correspendent of the "Western Mercury" tells an anecdote of Oliver Wendell Holmes. When he was in England in 1886 he found himself on one occasion at a" crush" in London amongst a great mass of people, including several Royal personages. He sat quietly in a corner, but presently feeling a little faint, and observ- ing refreshments in the distance, he turned to an elderly personage standing near, whom he supposed to be a butler or something of that kind, and asked for a harmless beverage. The supposed servant brought this with great alacrity, and remarked, "I am vary glad to meet you, Dr. Holmes." The Autocrat of the Breakfast Table was a little taken aback, and the stranger added, "I am Prince Christian." "Dear me," said Holmes, alive at once to the joke, "I have not had much acquaintance with princes, and, do you know, I took you for the waiter l" At this Prince Christian went off into into a burst of merriment. " Where is my wife," he said. "I must tell her this. She admires you im- mensely." Off went Prince Christian to fetch the Princess, and the genial American philosopher was soon the centre of a circle of Royalty, greatly delighted by the incident.

div.head: MODERN. CAVE-DWELLERS.
div.p: MODERN. CAVE-DWELLERS.
THE LATEST SOCIAL EXPERIMENT.

Dalziel says that arrangements are now being com- pleted for the formation of a curious colony next spring, the progress of which will be watched with interest. The leader of the movement is the Paris paper " Gravelle," and the idea is that by returning to the early and natural state of man human beings can live a life of ease and pleasure without work, and entirely independent of the trammels of civilisation. Some land has been procured in Auvergne, consisting mostly of chesnut forests, well supplied with water and furnished with commodious caves. Here five men and a like number of women will take up their habitations in a few months' time, living together in a natural state.and clothing themselves with the skins of beasts. Bread they will not make, for they consider it unnecessary, and its place will be taken by chesnuts. Water is to be their beverage, though they have no objection to cider and wine. They have been unable to renounce tobacco. A doctor they do not expect to require, and they will live either in huts or caves, according to the season of the year. The land to be allotted them measures eight hectares, and they compute that one hectare of land inhabited by game will yield a thousand kilos of meat yearly. Before taking possession they are going to well stcck the plantations with rabbits, pigs, cows, goats and fowls, which will all live in a wild state, and will be pre- vented from escaping into more civilised quarters by an impenetrable fence.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, MAGAZINES, ETC.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, MAGAZINES, ETC.

°ABSEIL AND CO.—The second yearly volume of " Chums " is now for sale, and we think it no exaggeration to say that it is quite the equal, and in some respects superior, to the last edition. Over a thousand illustrations and twelve coloured and tinted plates are included in this volume. The number of serial stories is somewhat unusual, viz. B,from the pens of the foremost caterers to the, boyish mind, of the day. Short stories, articles on swimmers, authors, athletes, &c., there are a host of, whilethe vein of humour also takes a promin- ent position. "Chums" for 1894 could not bum- celled as a gift book for boys, and for that meter girls, the majority of whom are as ready for a stir- ringstory as the most imaginative boy. This years issue is much handier in size and shape than the previous edition, while the tasteful and substantial binding is in every way suitable to the nature of its contents.—From the same publishers we have,to hand,the annual volume of the "Quiver," bound in a style due to the best "monthly" for Sunday and general reading. It contains 960 pages of the best letterpress by Eminent divines and popular authors a very large number of delicately-executed illustrations; five serial stories,and an innumerable quantity of storyettes, devotional and instructive papers,&c. An admirable coloured picture prefaces the volume. The published price is 7s. 6d.—A new volume of the "Magazine of Art" has its initiative in the November number. Two beautiful etchings entitled " Wooing " and "The Vale of Avoca" are included, together with a retrospect, articles on art in various forms, &c. Monthly, is. 4d. SIMPKIN, MARSHALL, HAMILTON AND KENT, LIMITED.—A very neat little 6d. book entitled "The Fansh awe Treasure" has been issued by the above well-known publishers. The author is Mrs. Qiiineey Lane (Leena) who is such a favourite with readers of all ages. Though small,the book is very prettily got up, the type being large, clear, and printed on good paper. T. _FISHER UNWlN.—Snirr, exceptionally good characteristics are published with the November number of "The Century." The two chief are a new novel by F. Marion Crawford entitled" Casa Braccio " which bids fair to become of absorbing interest, and an original " Life of Napoleon Bona- parte" by William M. Sloane. The commencement of the latter deals with the revolutionary epoch in Europe, Corsican politics and revolts, the Bona- panes in Corsica, the great emperor's birth and infancy, his schooldays, and his life in Paris and Valence. Portraits of himself, his parents, his home, and scenes in which he figures, are given to illustrate the biography. A new volume is also co mmenced with this part.

div.head: DEATH OF NELSON.
div.p: THE DEATH OF NELSON.

It was about twenty-five minutes past one, and Nelson and Hardy were pacing together, to and fro. The two had arrived within one.pace of the regular turning-spot at the cabin ladder-way, when Nelson (who, regardless of quarter-deck etiquette, was walking on the larboard side) suddenly faced left about. Hardy turned almost at the same instant, and saw him in the act of falling. A. musket-ball had struck him on the left shoulder, b the edge of the epaulet, cut through the spine, and buried itself in the muscles of the back towards the right side. Ile dropped at once upon hi, side, on the spot yet red with the blood of poor Scott. Seeker, a sergeant of Marines, and two privates, ran forward to nick him up. "They have done it at last Hardy," said Nelson, as he was lifted. "I hope not." " Yes ; my backbone is shot through." Yet even now he had presence of mind, as they were carrying him down to the cockpit, to observe that the tiller-ropes, which had been shot away, were not yet replaced, and to order that new ones should be rove immediately. He next ordered his bearers to cover his face with a handkerchief that the crew might not recognise him ; but the precaution was vain. The news was all over the ship in a minute. Many wounded officers and about forty men were being carried below at the same time; among them,Lieutenant Rann and Me, whipple, the Captain's clerk, who had actually-been killed by the wind of a shot. He was sent down to see if the tiller-ropes had been replaced. Yowl. Westphall—afterwarrls Sir George—to whom the question was put, was about to answer it, when a shot passed Whipple, and with e soh he fell down dead. Re had neither scratch nor mark upon him. A second after Westphall was wounded in the head. At the foot of the ladder the purser met the wounded Admiral, and had him carried over the heaps nf wounded and laid upon the purser's mattress, on the larboard side, close by Westphall, who lay there waiting for his wound to be dressed. Somebody rolled up the Admiral's coat and placed it under the head of the youngster, who was bleeding freely, so that when he was removed it was found that the bullion of Nelson's epaulet adhered to the coagulated blond, and it had. to he cut away. It was claimed by another man. Lieutenant Pascoe, who also lay wounded close by, and on his rrcovery he had the niece of gold set in a brooch with the motto of Trafalgar Day around it. . . . Down in .th cockpit of the Vietoey the surgeon soon perceived that Nel.on's wound was mortal. Nelson himself was eeetain of this frose the first, and insisted that Surgeon Beatty should go and attend to others • "for," said he, "you' can do nothing for me." His sufferings from pain and thirst were very great, and all that could be done was to fan him with . . . . .
