paper and give him lemonade from time to time. He kept asking for Hardy, that he might know how the fight went; but Hardy could not leave the deck at this most critical stage of the fight, and it was more than an hour before he thought it right to go below. Nelson began to think he must be dead, and repeatedly cried, "Will no one bring Hardy to me! He muse be killed! he is surely dead ! " Hardy's aide-de-camp, Mr. Bulkly, came down to the cockpit, and told the surgeon the reasons that detained the captain, but promised that he would take the first opportunity to leave the deck. "Who brought the message?" Nelson inquired, for his sight was dim. "Mr. Bulkly, my lord." "I thought I knew the voice. Bulkly, remember me to your father." And now even to those in the cockpit the result of the action began to de- clare itself. As often as a ship struck, the crew of the Victory sent up a cheer, and at every hurrah a gleam of joy passed over the face of the dying Admiral. When at length Hardy came down and took his hand in silence, Nelsan's first question was, " How goes the day with us ?" "Very well, my lord. We have taken ten ships; but five of their van have tacked and mean to bear down on us ; but I have called two or three of our fresh ships round, and have no doubt of giving them a drubbing." "None of ours have struck, I hope 2" " There is no fear of that." "I am a dead man, Hardy, lam going fast; it will be all over with me soon." Hardy tore himself away and ran up on deck, unable , to any longer to hold back his tears. Soon after the Victory opened her larbourd guns upon Rear-Admiral Dumanoir's squadron passing to windward. The concus- sion of Cie iirMg ii 'I the cockpit. " Oh, Victory, Victory! how you distract my poor brain." After a short pause he added, "How dear is life to all men ! " By this time all feeling below the breast was gone. In another fifty minutes Hardy come down to the cockpit again, and, again taking the hand of his dying friend and commander, congratulated him on a complete victory. How many of the enemy were taken he did not know, as it was impossible to see them distinctly through the smoke, but fourteen or fifteen at least. "That's well," cried Nelson ; " but I bargained for twenty." Then, in a stronger voice, " Anchor, Hardy —anchor !" "I have sent Lieutenant Hill to Lord Col- lingwood, who, I suppose, will now take upon himself the direction of affairs." " Not whilst I live, Hardy— no other man shall command whilst I live !" He tried to raise himself up from his pallet. " Anchor, Hardy, anchor !" Hardy was returning to deck when Nelson called him back and begged him to bend close. He then delivered his last injunctions—that- his hair might be cut off and given to Lady Hamilton, and that his body might not be thrown overboard, but taken home to Eng- land and buried beside his parents, unless the king should moller otherwise. "Take care of my dear Lady Hamilton; take care of poor Lady H tmilton !" Last of all he begged Hardy to kiss him. "Kiss me, Hardy," said he. Hardy knelt down and kissed his cheek and forehead. " Who is that ?" "It is Hardy, my lord." "God bless yeu, Hardy 1" Hardy now lett him for the last time. Nelson was turned on his right side, and death was now rapidly approaching. He muttered some inarticulate sentences, ending, " Remember that I leave Lady Hamilton and my daughter Horatia as a legacy to my country." Then once or twice he was heard to murmur to himself, " I have done my duty; I praise God for it." These were his last words. At half-past four, three hours and a quarter after he had received his wound, Nelson of the Nile was dead.—" The Story of the Sea."
ELECTION OF MAYOR.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held at the Town Hall on Friday at noon for the purpose of electing the mayor and committees for the ensuing year. The Mayor (Aid. Greenall) presided, and there were also present— Aldermen Francomb,Harrison, Wright, Hutchinson, Bolton, Sutton' Blackhi rat; Councillors Roberts, Shaw Green, Cannell, Lee, Hill, Woods, Muir, Plumpton, Heaton, H..oherd, Monks, Davies, Smeihurst, Shillcock, Skelton, Longton, Shaw, Baird, Greening, Evans,Pierpoint, R. T Fairclough, Wilkinson, J. Fairclougb, Bennett, Garner ;J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk),Fairhurst, (treasurer), Longdin (borough surveyor), Dr. Gornall (medical officer), Madeley (librarian). A large numberof the public were also present.
Councillor DAVIES supported. He also thought that the Liberal party ought to have its fair share on the committee.
Alderman GREENALL also thought that the Liberal party was entitled to another seat upon the committee, and he heartily supported the noncin ttion of Councillor Monks.

Alderman SUTTON said that be was always in favour of generisity to his opponents,and he supported Councillor Roberts' motion, although he thought that Aid. Hutchin- son was entitled to he upon the committee. Alderman FRANCOMB said that Alderman Hutchinson had informed him that he was willing to retire in favour of Councillor Monks. If Councillor Roberts would always govern his temper as he had done that day, he would be an exceedingly strong man in the Council. He would be pleased to see him upon the Watch Committee, and if he were he would then know that the members did their duty. During the time that he (Alderman Francomb) had been on the committee, he had never known anything to be done which he should be ashamed of being known by the whole town. The motioß of Councillor Roberts then became the substantive motion, owing to Councillor Hepherd with- drawing his nomination of Aldeman Hutchinson, and it was carried unanimously.

THE REMAINING COMMITTEES. The remaining committees were then elected unani- mously. The only changes to those we mentioned last week were that Alderman Hutchinson retired from the Town Hall &c. Committee in favour of Councillor Davies ; and Councillor R. T. Fairclough retiring from the Rivers Committee in favour of Alderman Hutchin- son. Councillor Fairclough stated as the cause of thiq step that there were reasons which prevented him from acting as chairman during a portion of the preceding year, and he found that there were reasons which would prevent him from doing so during the coming year.

div.head: MR. BALFOUR'S -REPLY TO LORD ROSEBERY.
div.p: MR. BALFOUR'S -REPLY TO LORD ROSEBERY.

Mr. Balfour addressed a great meeting at Newcastle on Tuesday evening on the subject of the House of Lords. He said that at this moment they were absolutely in the dark as to what the Government proposed in regard to that House, except that they intended to proceed by resolution in the House of Commons. What was there, he asked, to prevent their successors in governmene re versing or ignoring this resolution, just as they them- selves had reversed and ignored decisions of the House of Commons? When he looked at the course which the Government had pursued in Parliament he was driven to the conclusion that, whatever object they put second, they put first this campaign against the House of Lords, and he asked whether their action in dropping the Em- ployers' Liability Bill could have any other explanation than that they were much more anxious to excite public opinion against their colleagues in the House of Lords than they were to benefit the working classes. It was because the Lords had preformed certain functions of use to the general community, and for no other reason, that he did not desire to see their function as members of a Second Chamber cut short by the hand of these amateur revolutionists. The House of Lords had attained a power of adapting themselves by the natural operation of a silent growth to the new necessities in which they found themselves, and they would look back in vain on the action of that House since 1867 for any- thing which could be twisted into a desire to resist the settled will of the community. The right hon. gentle- man concluded by declaring that the House of Lords was to be sacrificed simply because the Newcastle pro- gramme had proved a failure. Addressing an overflow meeting, Mr. Balfour said that if the House of Lords was abolished the Union between Great Britain and Ireland would hang by a thread.

TH' MAYOR'S PROCESSION. Lads! aw've just bin to see a procession, Ov a Fat Corporation to Church; To make—az aw thowt—intercession, Fer keepin' Owd Nick i' the lurch! Aw ne'er seed a seet so imposin', An' th' creawd wur like sand on th' sea shore; Wile befoer aw cud get my owd nose in. Mi ribs wur aw squozzen an' sore! Fost ov aw coom a fine lot o' peelers— Sum caws urn "Invisible Blues " Ez a terror to "pickers an' stealers," An' givin' rnirauders ther dues. Th' "short an' th' lung" on't commanded, To watch ev'ry stride az thay went • An' aw wudn't meet them single-handed, If aw wur on wickedness bent! The next wur a sojers' battalion, Led up by a captain full weight ; An' thay praunc'd like a weel-to-dn stallion, An' look'd likely lads fer a feight ! Wi' sum drum an' fife magic to cheer 'urn, Playin' Ireland's favourite tune: But it duzn't quite suite me to hear 'um. Fer it upsets mi inside PO soon ! Then the Fire Brigade—aw good lookin,'— Coom up i' ther battle array: An' fer fear that sum chimbleys wur smookin,' Kept turnin' ther yeds ev'ry way. Thay're a credit to th' Borough, that's sartin,' An' no praise o' mine cud be higher: But aw hope thay'l ne'er need t' he divartin,' Ther skyowses on my heause-on-fire ! Next a Band wi' sum fine silver trumpets Coom on wi' a bang an' a jaw; It wur plain thay'd bin noan fed on crumpets, Er thay cudn't ha' made such a row. The chap that perform'd on th' Cornopean, Show'd uz aw wot fine fettle he'r in; Wile the Drummer, unlike th' Ethiopian, lied sumheaw bin changin' his skin! Make way for His Wership, yo thrutchers ! That grand chain an' geawn mun be seen; Yore welly ez close ez thonse " touchers" That's play'd on a nayburin' green. NIP His Wership a tall mon wur walkin,' A lawyer one diver 'an sed ; Fer he favver't weel cut eaut fer talkie,' Becoze ov aw th' wool on his yed ! The Aldermen mostly coom after, Aw deck'd ther holiday trim; An' the Ceauncillors, sum wild wi' laughter, An' sum lookin' terribly grim. Wi' a fine burly joker woze notion Aw'm sure was to do um aw good; An' to teych urn perpetooal motion, For puttin' urn rest wi' ther blood! When the organ an' choir bed bin singin' The sollum an' softenin' notes ; An' the anthems an' chants hod done ringin - Fro charmin' an' musical throats ; Then the parson begun wi' his teychin,' An' gen it us aw hot an' strung ; God bless his white yed fer his preychin,' An' not makin' th' sarmon so lung. Ther was only one cross to mi pleasure, Wen a folly i'th' pew be-it me, Kept bawkin' an' groanin, full measure, I' strugglin' to reych double D! After aw, aw'll noan fail at confessin' Aw felt it wur good to be theer' • An' aw hope, wi' kind Providence blessin', Aw'll be wi yo once moor next year. TUN! 0' PEGS.
Rose Bonk, November 16th, 1894.

div.head: RETIRING MAYOR RETURNS THANKS.
div.p: THE RETIRING MAYOR RETURNS THANKS.

The Mayor said that he received the resolution kindly passed at the last meeting of the Council for his servises as Mayor. He regretted that he had not been able to be present at that meeting, but he would like to express his gratitude for what that resolution was intended to convey. He was wishful to thank the Council for the assistance they had given him during his term of office. In an assembly of that kind it was not possible always to go on smoothly, but he asked on behalf of his successor that they would extend to him all the kind consideration and patience which he had invariably received at their hands. (Applause.) He also thanked the inhabitants of the town for the great courtesy and good feeling which had been shown to him throughout his term of office. He also thanked the officials for their willing assistance. In conclusion he regretted that he would not be able to give the assistance he would like to the future Mayor, as unfortunately the doctor had ordered him away from England for the next six months.

div.head: ELECTION OF MAYOR.
div.p: ELECTION OF MAYOR.

Alderman SUTTON said that it was his pleasing duty to propose the following resolution: "That James Fair- dough, a councillor for the time being, be elected Mayor for the ensuing year, and until the acceptance of office by his successor." He said that he did not think it was at all necessary for him in any way to allude to the qualifications of Mr. Fairclough for that important office. He was a native of Warrington. and they all knew him very well. Since he had become a member of the Council, he had worked honestly and faithfully for the town. His gentlemanly conduct, and genial and kind disposition on all occasions, had won the esteem of every one. He was quite sure that his qualifications were sufficient to entitle him to fill the office not only creditably to himself, but to the credit of the town. (Applause.) Councillor ROBERTS, as seconder of the nomination at the caucus meeting of the Council, said that he had great pleasure in seconding it in public. Everything Alderman Sutton had said was fully and cordially en- dorsed on that side of the house. They recognised in Councillor Fairclough, a gentleman not only associated largely in one of the most prominent of the industries of the town, but one who, in his private capacity, had always acted fairly, honourably, and straightforwardly. They had every confidence that, as chief magistrate of the borough, he would carry out that responsible and onerous duty in the spirit of fairness, and they only hoped that his health might be robust enough to bear that most serious responsibility. He was sure that every member of the Council, and every inhabitant of War- rington would render Councillor Fairclough every assist- ance that lay in their power. He would like to express on behalf of other members of the Council, the deep regret they felt at the illness of the Mayor (Alderman dreenall). They were extremely glad to see him there that day, and that he was better than he had been for some time. He hoped that when he returned after his comparative retirement, he would be restored to health again. (Applause.) Alderman }Lummox supported the motion, which was carried with applause. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH then retired to the ante-room where he was invested with the robes of office, and after returning to the Council Chamber, he took the chair amid great applause. He said that he thanked them for the honour which they had conferred upon him by electing him Mayor for the ensuing year. He trusted that he would be able to perform his duties to the satis- faction of the members of the Council and the inhabitants of Warrington. At the same time he would like to ask of them to assist him, as it would help him materially to conduct the business in an orderly manner, and would make his duties a pleasure to him. (Applause.) The MAYOR then appointed Alderman Greenall the deputy Mayor, and the Rev. E. C. E, Carleton his chap- lain. He invited all those present to accompany him to the parish church on Sunday morning,and if the weather was unfavourable, he would take care that they would have conveyances.
ELECTION OF THE WATCH COMMITTEE.-AMICABLE ARRANGEMENT.

Alderman HARRISON moved the election of the Mayor, Aldermen Harrison, Blackhurst, Francomb, Wright, and Sutton ,Councillors Cannel!, Greening,Heaton,aud Davies upon the Watch Committee. Alderman BLACIIIIIIRST seconded. Councillor DAVIES said that he would like to withdraw his name, as there was some feeling that a solicitor should not be upon the Watch Committee. Of course he did not agree with that idea, as he thought that a lawyer had more right upon it than a magistrate. It was a great mistake for a magistrate to be on the com- mittee, as he simply travelled from there to the police court thus hearing the case twice over.l Councillor HEPHERD proposed that Alderman Hutchin- son be elected in the place of Councillor Davies.

Alderman BOLTON seconded. Alderman SUTTON said that he could not let the re- marks of Councillor Davies go by unchallenged. The i magistrates did not take any part n any case before it went before the bench at the police court. Councillor ROBERTS said that he moved the adoption of another name. He quite agreed that neither a magis- trate nor anybody else shouid hear a case twice over,and also that no case should be heard before the Watch Com- i ttee. Aldermen SUTTON and HARRISON rose and denied that the cases were heard before the Watch Committee. Councillor ROBERTS (continuing) said that that was by the way. He was going to make an appeal, and he hoped he would not hurt the susceptibilities of any member of the Council. They had begun the new year ley the unanimous election of the mayor, and so far as he (Councillor Roberts) was concerned, he wished to see everything carried through with all the good temper that was possible. He hoped there would be no em- bittered discussion upon the nomination of any gentle- man to the committee. He wished to propose the ap- pointment of Mr. Wm. Pierpoint, and he did it without any feeling of dis egard to Alderman Hutchinson, who had been a member of the Council for many years, and had served it faithfully and well. He simply wished to ask the dominant majority of the Council to exercise that spirit of fairness! and English cansideration, which was always shown to opponents by asking them that seeing that the Liberal members of the Council num- bered rather more than a quarter of the entrie Coun- cil- Councillor SHAW (interrupting) : They are of superior intelligence. The MAYOR asked Councillor Shaw to allow Councillor Roberts to proceed, and not interrupt him in that manner. - - - -

Councillor ROBERTS (continuing) said that seeing also that at present they had only one representative out of ten upon the Committee, it would only be fair that the Conservative Majority should give them one more seat, which would then only give them one-fifth of the entire number of the Committee. In regard to Councillor Pierpoint's qualifications, he had been a member of the Committee, and had served nine years in the Council. He was largely associated with the business of the town, and he had the necessary experience and ability for a seat on the Committee. He might be told that the majority must rule. That remark was made a genera- tion ago, and most of the members of the Corporation of that time were no longer in their midst. Alderman Harrison was the only one who still remained, and he hoped he would be with them for many years to come. Were they going to let the ill-feeling continue for ever? Let the dead past bury its dead, and let them have a consideration for their opponents becoming to members of the Council. He was not going to say that the majority was not entitled to rule over the Council, but he asked them to give those who were weak something of their strength, and let the Liberal minority have some share in the governing of the town. He asked the Con- servative majority not to leave a legacy of distrust and dislike to their successors. He hoped that the Conser- vatives would yield to his appeal, but if they were determined to resist it. the Liberals wo•ald have to abide by it, and wait until their time should come. (Applause.) Councillor SHAW-GREEN seconded the appointment of Councillor Pierpoint. He thought that the spirit of compromise which ruled English institutions should pre- vail, and that the members would meet the appeal of Councillor Roberts, by substituting Mr. Pierpoint for Mr. Davies.

Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH supported Councillor Roberts' motion. He thought that the Liberal party had not their fair share upon the committee, and it was only proper that they should have one more seat. Councillor Roberts had struck at the keynote of the whole thing, and he thought the constitution of the committee should be made with fairness to each party. Alderman BOLTON said that he did not understand how the matter stood. He thought that Councillor Pier. point had refused to be nominated at the caucus meeting. The MAyou said that be had not refused, but had said that he did not care to he on the committee.

At this stage Councillor Pierpoint walkcd over to Councillor Roberts, and after a short private conversa- tion, Councillor ROBERTS said that he would propose another name which would solve the difficulty. Coun- cillor Pierpcint had consented to retire in favour of Councillor Monks. He had, therefore, great pleasure in proposing Councillor Monks for the seat on the com- mittee. Alderman BLACKHURST seconded.

div.head: PRESIDING ALDERMEN.
div.p: PRESIDING ALDERMEN.

On the motion of the MAYOR, secr4nded by Alderman GREENALL, it was decided to allot the aldermen to pre- side over the various wards as follows :—Town Hall ward, Alderman Greenall ; Whitecross, Alderman Hutchinson; Bewsev, Alderman Holmes; Orford, Alder- man Harrison ; Fairfield. Alderman Wright ; Howley, Alderman Francomb ; St. Austin's, Alderman Black- burst; Latchford, Alderman Bolton, This concluded the business.

div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN T WARRINGTON.

The gas question is still to the fore in Warrington, and many are the inquiries as to the cause of the poor light which we are having,now that tha nights are getting longer. The Gas Committee has been "called over the coals" time after time, but still there is very little—if any—improvement. One would have thought after Alderman Harrison had been compelled to go to bed at half-past nine in the evening in consequence of the bad light, that the committee would have mended their ways. They have not improved, however, and I have been told by a friend who lives in Latchford—where the gas appears to be the worst—that c,ne night he had to get a candle to read by. Yet our gas is supposed to illuminate at the rate of "18 point something"candle power. I think it is quite time that something was done to remedy this state of affairs, for gas is very dear in Warrington, in comparison with a good number of towns round about.

I don't think that Warrington has 'ever before been favoured with a lecture on Socialism by a lady, but such was the case on Thursday evening at a meeting promoted by the local branch of the Inde- pendent Labour Party. I suppose she would be styled by some people one of the "New Women" and they would be as unkind in their remarks about her as the epigrammatist who termed the New Woman: "a fresh darn in the blue stocking." But, whatever else may be said, Miss Martyn is a fine lecturer—or is it lecturess ? The title of the lecture delivered was "Municipal Socialism," and, coupled with a thorough knowledge of her subject, she had an excellent delivery. She spoke greatly in favour of School Boards, and on this question she was well qualified to speak, having, as she stated, been employed as teacher in both Voluntary and Board Schools. She urged that workingmen and women should be representatives upon local bodies in order to force the carrying out of measures which bad been passed for the benefit of the working classes, and commented strongly on the fact that men who were interested in keeping insanitary property had seats on Town Councils, and voted fir its continuance. Of course, a remark of this kind could have no reference to the War- rington Town Council—no, not in the remotest degree. We all know that.

div.head: CHARGE OF NEGLECTING CHILDREN AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: CHARGE OF NEGLECTING CHILDREN AT WARRINGTON.

On Friday,'the magistrates at the Borough Court heard a charge of neglect of five children preferred against William Beckett,slater, residing at 15 Keen- street, made by Inspector McAteer, N.S.P.C.C. Mr. Buckton, solicitor, who prosecuted on behalf of the societv,stated that Inspector McAteer made a visit to the defendant's house on the 19th September and there saw that neglect of children was going on. He warned the defendant, and on visiting the defendant's house on several occasions afterwards he found that a slight improvement was made. The improvement, however, did not last, and in a very short time the house and the condition of the children became worse than ever. There were five children, the oldest being 15 years of age, and the youngest 4 years. The man who was a widower, was earning about 30s. a week as a slater. There was no furniture in the house and the man's earnings were mostly spent in gambling and drink. There was no bedding for the chitdren to lie on. They were ensured for a penny each per week, and that made the defendant liable to a heavier penalty. Inspector McAteer stated that on the 19th Sept., in company with P.C. Rylatt, he visited the defend- ant's house and they found two children—the oldest and the youngest—with their father in the house. The eldest girl,Martha, was wearing two torn garments and portion of a chemise. Her hair was matted and covered with knits and vermin. The child, May, four years of age, was also in a filthy condition. No food was found in the cupboard, and the rooms were very dirty. rhe bedding consisted of a rickety iron bedstead, an old mattrass,but no brd covering. The floor was saturated with urine and excrement. The house smelt abomin- ably. He sent for Dr. Bowden, who examined the house and certified it as being filthy. The defendant on being questioned as to how he accounted for such a state of things, said that his daughter, who was 15 years of age, would not do anything for him, and he intended to get married shortly. Witness called again on three other occasions, and told defendant what would be the con- sequence if he did not improve the condition of the house and children. Defendant promised that he would get , some beds and bedding. He did get one new iron bed- stead and some bedding for himself, but none for the 'children. On his last visit the house and children were as bad if not worse than at his first visit.—P.C.'s Rylatt and Barnett gave evidence as to the neglect of the children, and the dirty condition of the house.—Dr. Bowden was away on his holidays,and unable to appear. The defendant stated that he had been a staunch teeto- taler for eleven years. His wages were very irregular and during the last fornight he had only earned 233. 6d. altogether. He buried his wife some time ago, and he had been unable to look after the children when woi king or leaking for work. He had to depend upon his eldest girl looking after them. But he had made up his mind to marry again and he thouett that then his children would not be neglected.—William Jones, brother-in-law, said he had been visiting the defendant's house for the last four or five years. He did not think that the children had been badly neglected. The defen- dant was a teetotaler, and was " guard" of the local Good Templars Order. The defendant did not earn 30s. week as stated. The magistrates decided to adjourn the case for one month.

BETTING RAID AT WARRINGTON. POLICE COURT PROCEEDINGS.

At about nine o'clock on Thursday evening,a raid was made upon the dwelling house of Mrs. Mather, 16 Friars Green,by the Warrington police, who ap- parently suspected that betting was going on over the Liverpool races. The chiefs of the police in charge of the arrangements were Mr. S. Hunt (chief constable), Inspectors James,Spinks and Cox,Detec- tive Sergeant Monaghan, and Sergeants Cheney and Chantler. The raid was carried out in a very expe- ditious manner, and great excitement prevailed at the time. Mrs. Mather, her son, William Mather, and her daughter,Annie Mather, besides the follow- ing six men : Charles Gough, 5, River-road, Michael Barry, 5 Bakehouse-yard, William Thomas, 10 New- road, Martin Jordan, 43 Ann-street,George Newton, 37 Laira-street, and Thomas Brookes, 15 Laira- street,and others, were conveyed to the police stat- ion in a bus. The police also secured £l2O in money, a cheque for £43, and a large number of books, and racing cards. After examination, the party were liberated on bail at 10.30. The police appear to have taken the occupants of the house completely by sur- prise,and the whole party were captured, but some of them were aeemed too young, and' were set at liberty. It is stated that amongst the papers which fell into the hands of the police was a note contain- ing a warning that the house was to be " raided " that evening. POLICE PROCEEDINGS. There was a large crowd outside the police station yesterday morning when the party were brought before the magistrates. The charge against Sarah Ann Mather was that of keeping a house at 16, Friar's-green for the purpose of betting under the meaning of the Gaming Act, on the Bth November, and divers other dates. William and Annie Mather were charged with assisting and using the house for the purpose of betting, and the remaining six defendants were charged with aiding and abetting the other defendants. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk) appeared on behalf of the police, Mr. Percy Davies for the defendants Mather, and Mr.Unsworth for Mitchael Barry. Mr. Davies said that the charge was a very serious one, and it would only be fair that an adjournment should be eranted. He was prepared to agree to that day week, if the magistrates would allow that. He had only seen Mr. Mather at twenty minutes to ten that morn- ing, and there had, therefore, been no time to go into anything. Be was prepared to offer £lOO bail. The Town Clerk said that he: had no objection what- ever to an adjournment. Mr. Davies said that £l2O had been seized,and he hoped that the £2O would be given to Mrs. Mather. Mr. Hunt said that he mustlkeep that meney, as he was responsible for it. Mr. Davies thought it was unfair to his clients. He thought £lOO was handsome bail,and his clients wanted money to get up their case. Mr. Pierpoint : Was this money found onithe pre- mises?

Mr. Hunt: The whole of the money was found in the room in which the betting was taking place. Mr. Davies contended that the keeping of the mosey would cripple the case for the defence. Every penny of their money was in the safe in the room. He was not going to take the case on credit. (Laughter.) Alderman Wright (chairman of the magistrates) said that they were disposed to support Mr. Hunt. It was finally decided that Mrs. Mather should give a receipt for the cheque of £43. and that the money seized should be retained. The case was then adjourned until next Friday.

After the parties had left the Court Mr. Davies re- turned and informed the magistrates that the supposed cheque of £45, was in reality fer rent paid two years ago. He therefore repeated his application for £2O cash,which the magistrates declined to accede to.

LECTURE ON "MUNICIPAL SOCIALISM" AT WARRINGTON. At the Co-operative Hall on Thursday last week before a fair audience, Miss Martyn, of the London Fabian Society, delivered a lecture on "Municipal Socialism." The meeting was under the auspices of the Warrington branch of the Independent Labour Party, and the chair was occupied by Mr. J. Matthews. He briefly commented on the progress made by the In- dependent Labour Party, and referred to its objects. Miss Martyn at the outset of her lecture explained what was meant by Socialism. Instead of the individualism of the present day which was for each person to do the best he could for the individual self, they wished to substitute for that "each for all and all for each." They wished to destroy the anarchy of individual competition and substitute co-operation and organisation. Referring to the importance of workingmen having their represen- tatives on local administrative bodies,she pointed out that there were excellent laws regarding the housing of the working-classes but they were never enforced because workingmen had as their representatives a number of men who were interested in property. The municipality was empowered to build decent houses, but was it likely that these men would support a scheme which would cause their houses—and some of them insanitary houses —to come in competition with houses built by the municipality. It was to such men's interest to maintain them as they were. Besides working for the reform of the personnel of the House of Commons they must work for the reform of the personnel of the local bodies. They had had lessons that year with regard to the elections of local bodies. They found that the Conservatives would join with the Liberals to throw out the Trades Council men, the Independent labour men, or the Socialists. It had been done in town after town. The lecturer con- sidered that women should also be elected on local thorities. Just as women were needed in the home so were they needed in the city life. They needed the in- fluence of women on local bodies. She urged them to do what they could to secure the representation of women on their own put-Ale authorities. She then referred to the dwellings of the working classes as at present constructed, and contrasted them with what they should be. She contended that all municipalities should pay the Trades Union rate of wages and stated that the London County Council never paid its workers less than 245. per week for a man, and 18s. per week for a woman. Dealing with the education question she said her experience in both Church and Board schools led her to be in favour of the Board schools. When teaching in a school she was told by one of the lady managers that what they wanted the children to do was to just pass the examination and get the Gov- ernment grant. Too much education was not good for them. She was then a member of the Primrose League and able to be taken into full confidence. (Laughter.) The lecturer also spoke of the importance of having working,men and women representatives on the 'Parish Councils and Board of Guardians. At the conclus- ion of the lecture questions were solicited. In reply to a question as to the method of dealing with the unem- ployed, Miss Martyn said one way, was to oblige the municipal bodies to provide work by starting relief works, and then to see that they were always prepared. with work, and that the standard rate of wages was enforced. By this means the unemployed would gradu- ally be absorbed. In reply to another question she said she was in favour of the municipalisation of the drink traffic. They could then reaulate the traffic, provide purer drinks, and other refreshments. There was also an economical side as well as a moral side in favour of the traffic being in the hands of the municipal bodies. A collection was taken in aid of the funds of the local branch of the Independent Labour Party.

div.p: WHAL SHALL WE DO W LTA THE LORDS?
(A Duet:for one voice).

What shall we (11 with the Lords'? Is such a tip-tepical question: Their existence all progress retards, Thus threatening the bulwarks we rest on. Their character Feudal, their state non-eleclive, Reduce to a "farce," that's for " laughter' effective, Our "Popular Government," " Freedom " perfective! Says-I to myself, sir, says I. What shall we do with the P,.ers ?

Sure. now we've no Representation, Since gilded Heredity's jeers Can veto the will of the nation ! What boots waste of time, and Election'expenses, The' hustings,"the"franchise,"and such vain pretences While a few Irresponsibles can set spiked fences, To thwart all our millions ! says I. What shall we do with the Lords ?

How burst the strong shackL.s of knay'ry ? Our present position accords With naught but political slav'ry— An illogical boL!gle of stultification, A crisis unmatched in its humiliation_ Unworthy the name of our people and nation, Says I to myself, says I. This then, must we do with the Peers , Let's build a big special museum, Wherein we may fix them in tiers, And label, that poor folks may see 'urn ; Then hire some rare lecturer on Archmology, Who'll point out their "mnr*s," in ornate terminology, As the latest survivals of Feudal " phiz "-ology ! Says I to myself, sir, says I.

THAT Lord ROSEBERY has lost none The Premier on Polities. of his popularity in Scotland by his

accession to the Liberal leader- ship was once more emphasised by the remarkable meetings—one of them an over- flow meeting of formidable proportions —which he addressed in Glasgow on Wednes- day. His speech was worthy of the occasion. In it he dealt boldly and freely with the political situation, and, above all, it vibrated with the genuine fighting ring. It has been declared time after time by Tories, from Lord SALIS- BURY downwards Lord Rosumay does not mean "business," that lie has no real attachment to or desire to promote the policy of the party which he leads, and particular- ly that part of it which relates to the House of Lords. Lord SALISBURY has even gone so far as to declare that when the Premier speaks of the reform of the House of Lords he speaks with his tongue in his cheek. This is a license of imputation which Lord ROSEBERY justly resents, and declares to be outside not merely the courtesies and amenities but even the decencies of political life. After this reproof it may, perhaps, dawn upon the mind of the Tory leader that people may be really in earnest in other causes besides that of the • defence of, the extremest claims of property and privilege. No one questions Lord SALISBURY'S sincerity, except when he is dealing in a gingerly manner with some of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S semi- socialistic schemes. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is at the present time in ally who is too valuable to be lightly dispensed with, and,theref ore, Lord SALIS- BURY is under some compulsion to speak with a certain amount of respect of the Birmingham programme. At the same time it is quite easy to. see that a tone of unqualified denunciation would be more in harmony with his general bearing towards such subjects. In Lord ROSEBERY'S speech of Wednesday there was, at all events, no. ambiguous note. His position with regard to the subjects he touched upon was clearly and firmly indicated. He again declared his adhesion to the cause of Scotch disestablishment though he held out little hope of the subject being effectually dealt with in this Parliament. As he pointed out Wales has a prior claim in connection with dises- tablishment. The demand for disestablishment in the Principality is more extensive and more decisive than it is in Scotland. Out of thirty- four Welsh members thirty-one demand that the Church which is alien to them in every respect shall be disestablished. It is true, Ithat Scotland has returned a majority of some- thing like five to two in the same cause, but, as

div.head: AY, NOVEMBER 17, 1894.
div.p: AY, NOVEMBER 17, 1894.
had much pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. On the motion of Dr. Steele seconded by Mr. T. T. Sill a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the High Sheriff for his attendance.

The bazaar was visited throughout Wednesday by large numbers of people amongst whom were many purchasers. The specially painted scenery was much admired, more particularly the paintings of the old parish:church, and the various portions which went to make up the Old Castle. The costumes of some of the stallholders were very handsome. Business proved very brisk considering the present depressed state of trade in the town, and the total amount realized on Wednesday was nearly £327. This has given general delight. On Thursday afternoon the sale was opened by Lady Brooke of Norton Priory, who appeared on the platform in the company of the hon. Miss Gladys Rice, the hon. Mrs. Britton, Mrs. Egerton Lee. Miss Cicely Halsey, Miss Florence Crawley, the Rev. Canon M. Wood, Mr. F. A. Lake, and Mr. John Banks. Lady Booke as introduced by Canon Wood and declared the bazaar open in the course of an appropriate address. She was then accorded a hearty vote of thanks on the proposition of Mr. Lake' seconded by Mr. Banks. The hall was again full, and bore every prospect of the second day being almost as successful as the first. Both on Wednesday and Thursday, concerts of a miscellaneous description were given at intervals, whilst choice selections of music were rendered by Mr. Ravens- croft's band of talented performers. A variety of other antertainments was also given by Mr. J. L. Wyman, the popular conjurer. TECHNICAL EDUCATION IN WARRINGTON.

div.head: WORK OF THE TECHNICAL INSTITUTE.
div.p: THE WORK OF THE TECHNICAL INSTITUTE.

The Technical Institute is now a familiar name in Warrington, but it is to be feared that, in spite of all the methods of advertising resorted to by the Committee and their indefatigable secretary, Mr. Madeley, it is still little more than a name with a good many people who might benefit from a more intimate knowledge. In fact, we may very safely hazard the statement that many people who think they know something about the work of the Insti- tute would be surprised, on a little closer acquaint- ance, by the extent and variety of the operations I carried on. On every night of the week, with thy exception of Saturdays and Sundays, there are numerous classes carried on at the Museum, the School of Art, the People's College, and at the old barracks in Wilson-Patten-street, now known as the School of Science. The scattering of the classes over so many different buildings is, of course, .a disadvantage, but under present circumstances it cannot be helped. When a fine block of buildings has been erected either by private generosity or public munificence the Institute will then have a fitting habitation, and all its classes will be con- centrated under one roof. But that happy time is not yet, is not even visible yet, so that if a person is privileged to have a glance at a number of the principal classes he must, as in the case of the writer of the present article, do a fair amount of perambulation. Take a Monday evening, for instance. You drop into the School of Art any time between seven and eight and you find Mr. Aylward busy with a class in practical geometry. A fine class it appears to be, too, composed in about equal parts of young men and young women,several of whom are pupil teachers as this is one of the subjects to qualify for teaching drawing in the ele- mentary schools. When this class finishes its task another class commences for more advanced students, and there is still a third class for day students on Tuesday afternoons. Leaving the School of Art and going to the School of Science you manage to get to the upper storey of this interesting building by means of stairs which, to put it discreetly, are more suitable for a barracks or a medieval fortress than a School of Science. In one of the rooms here, Mr. F. G. Ruddock, F 1.C., is lecturing to a class upon the elements of iron and steel. The class is not a large one, but it is attentive. Considering the nature of the Warrington industries and the import- ance of the local iron trade the class might well be larger, and it would seem that there are young men in Warrington who are neglecting opportunities to acquire useful and profitable knowledge. From the School of Science to the Peoples' College is not a long distance, and the latter place one finds to be quite a centre of activity. Several classes, and nearly all of them well attended are here in full swing. These classes are in connection with the Continuation School—which along with the School of Art and the School of Science—constitutes the Technical Institute—and they are attended for the most part by students who, having left the ele- mentary school and commenced to work, wish to continue their education. In some instances the pupils are by no means of so juvenile an appearance as might be supposed. As showing the amount of teaching given it may be mentioned that there are no fewer than five teachers of arithmetic alone. They are all certificated and drawn from the local elementary schools, the superintendent of the Con- tinuation School being Mr. R. J. Hall of the People's College. In other parts of the People's College on a Monday evening there are also classes in French, preparatory and advanced, taught by Mdlle Blanchet, and in music, the teacher in this latter case being Mr. W. S. Wood. On a Tuesday evening there is an equally busy scene at all the buildings. In the School of Art Mr. Aylward and his assistants teach large classes in elementary model drawing, and at the School of Science Mr. Ruddock has a more advanced and a larger class in inorganic chemistry. Nearly all the students in tnis class are young men engaged in trades to which a knowledge of chemistry is directly applicable, and to judge by appearances they all "mean business." There are also a few young women in this class and they certainly appear to be no less in earnest than the other students. The lecture to this class is ilustrated with experiments. At the People's College there are again numerous classes. A class of between twenty and thirty is initiated by Mr. A. Perris into the mysteries of commercial correspondence—the writing of business lettere, the drafting of telegrams, &c., and the meaning of commercial terms and abbreviation. Is another room of the same building a large number of young girls are being instructed in needlework and in still other directions there are numerously attended classes for shorthand, for arithmetic, and for English composition. Coming back to the large room at the M useum,one finds that there is still one more subject being taught on this evening,and that islrnathematics. The teacher is Mr. W. H. Stens- field, and judging from the ready answers which he receives from his pupils, they are making satis- factory progress in this most abstruse of subjects. On Wednesday and Thursday evenings the classes are again numerous. On Wednesdays the pupils in cookery assemble under the tuition of Mrs. Cann, and as they are fairly numerous and appear to take a lively interest in their work, there is a bright prospect of improvement in the housewifery of the future. The learners are pot through a course of real cookery,and not mere make-believe,and the fin- ished product is either bought by the pupils, or, if left on band, it is handed over to Mrs. Carleton for charitable distribution. Another useful subject which is taught on this evening is that of book- keeping, the teacher being Mr. James Bolton. The class is well attended by youths to whom the infor- mation imparted will be useful in their every-day work. At the School of Science Sloyd woodwork is taught by Mr.F. C. Herzog. It is an interesting sub- ject,and although the chief object in view is that of training and the development of faculties, yet the skill in woodwork which is acquired by a course in this class must, one should thiuk,be useful in many ways. It is, therefore, to be regretted that she class is not largely attended. In the upper rooms of the same building on Wednesday evenings there are more classes in chemistry. One of them is in the advanced practical course, and each student is provided with a cupboard and apparatus for his own experiments. On. Friday evening two of the most important classes are those of machine draw- ing at the School of Art and dressmaking at the Museum. The class of machine drawing has steadily increased, and is now larger than it has ever been before. The dressmaking claes,under the tuition of Mrs. Dobson, is also a very fl)urishing one, and almost fills the lecture room at the Museum. Altogether, it will be seen that a great work is being done at the Technical Institute. It is satis- factory to know that there is a very consider able increase in the number of students this year over previous seasons,and in some directions the increase is very marked, There is still room for a very large growth.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

Last week I alluded to common rights and such like luxuries, and especially to the large tract of waste land called the.mesnes, and to the fact that by degrees it was being enclosed, the only portion left for the enjoyment (?) of the public being a fenced in footpath, so many feet wide. I have lately had ocaasion to traverse this footpath for the first time during several months, and to say that I was surprised at its condition, would be to put the matter very lightly. I can hardly express my feel- ings. I was disgusted, sir. Yes, thoroughly dis- gusted. I intended to ruminate whilst in the midst of green pastures,but my intentions were disagree- ably cut short—ruthlessly so, by suddenly plunging almost ankle deep in good English mud. I ejacu- lated, strongly, and gazing at the moon, thought I detected a smile, which I in my condition took to be contemptuous. Contempt at our slowness, in allowing without question ourselves to be fenced off into a few feet of slush. Somebody has taken upon themselves, rightly or wrongly, to lay out this footpath, and if he or they have a right to do this,l think in common humanity they should put the footpath in such a condition that Christians can use it comfortably. To me it became a slough of despond, and at every yard I despaired of finding any improvement. Here is a fine scope for a dis-; trict councillor aspirant to advertise himself.

But this is not the only spot in which mire exists in large quantities. I regret to say, that we have no need to wander so far as the mesnes to find English mud. It exists in all our principal streets, at least those of them which are made of macadam, such as Market-street, and Queen-street. I don't blame the macadam, because if properly and systematically attended to, that kind of road material can be made to be as clean and respectable as any other. lam perfectly certain that everyone will agree with me when I say that these two streets have lately been in a most deplorable condition. Of course I admit the weather has not been of the best, yet if you visit places where they take a pride in their streets, you will find that they take measures to obviate the bad effects of the weather.
Nou

Some people never have enough of a good thing. The good thing I allude to being six days in every week, on each of which we can do pretty much as we like, without injuring the proprieties. This is not enough for some classes of the community, for lately, Vitriol Square way, they have taken to en- croaching on the seventh, which according to tra- dition was given to us as a day of rest. Not so with those I refer to for they have transposed the read- ing, and interpret Sabbath to mean "recreation," thus Sabbath day or Sunday "Day of recreation." (Johnson). Consequently they engage in football matches—not a few lads kicking a ball about but a regular football match on Sunday afternoons, and they make the air hideous with their shouts, whilst respectable people are taking a quiet walk. Fortu- nately, the police have taken notice of such un- seemly behaviour, and have stepped in to inform these Sabbath desecrators that such a mode of passing Sunday. cannot be allowed in a civilised place like Earlestown. If calm reasoning won't put a stop to it, I should try forcible argument.

I have heard plenty of talk lately, about the "New woman," but so far, it has not been my good fortune to meet one. Thus I must plead ignorance as to her appearance• and general demeanour, but they tell me that slowly but Surely, this "new woman," is usurping the places and positions, held, from time immemorial, by men. Now I don't think there are any of the species round this quarter—at any rate they have not come prominently forward as yet—but some of the ordinary women, the usual style of women, are coming to the front with a vengeance. I dare say you have heard of the Women's Liberal Association, which, as I have no need to tell you, is composed solely of women. Well, these ladies, with the best of intentions, have called the male sex together and have offered to assist them in forming a " Men's Liberal Association," not an antagonistic affair, but to work in unison with the Women's, for the pur- pose of pushing forward the Liberal cause. So nicely was the matter put before them, that the men at once decided it was necessary to form such an association and they forthwith appointed a secretary temporarily. This looks like business, and, if successful, the Women's Liberal Association will deserve all the praise and credit all good Liberals can give them. GOOD TEMPLAR CoNVENTION AT EARLESTOWN.

The quarterly meeting of No. 1 Convention S.W. Lancashire was held in the schoolroom, Vulcan, on Saturday. The session was called to order by Bro. W. H. Dale, C.C.T. (Earlestown) who was supported by various officers, deputies, and representatives from lodges in the area of the Convention, the total attendance being over 50. After the opening Bro. Morris Jones, D. Sec. of Liverpool attended and was invited to preside during the remainder of the session. The usual press and Credential Committees were appointed, after which the 'reports of the officers were received. Bro. Dale, C.C.T. gave a very interesting report, but regretted his inability to visit the lodges lately, owing to pressure of other important duties. Bro. E. Newman C.Sec. reported a much improved position. The past quarter had been one of the most ac'ive in his recollection, and he was gratified to be able to report successful pro- gress, nearly every lodge reporting an increase in members. The Hope of Earlestown lodge had ad- vanced to 150 members, an increase of SS; the " Ebenezer " reported 43, increase 12, and the "hope of Vulcan' lodge, opened during August now reported 42 members. Up to date the lodges showed a total membership of 476, an increase of 73, with three lodges still to send in reports. Altogether the position and prospects of the order in the Convention area were extremely gratifying, and he trusted the earnestness and vigour mani- fested during the past few months might be con- tinuous. Tiro. G. E. Warburton. C.S.J.T. reported the Juvenile Templars generally to be active and doing good work. One senior temple at Leigh was not now meeting and there prospects of a new temple being opened shortly at the Vulcan. Bro. John Taylor. C.E. Supt. gave an interesting report of active efforts in adjourned licensing sessions and municipal elections,in various parts of the area, showing the question of dealing with the liquor traffic to have occupiei a prominent position. Bro. G. Tornlin,C. Treas ,reporte.d finances as satisfactory, with a balance in hani. All the reports,after some little discussiom, were adopted. It was deeided to hold the next session on December 15, the place of meeting being left for the Convention Executive to decide upon. Owing to executive duties, Bro. G.E. Warburton, C.S.J.T. felt compelled to resign his office. The resignation was accepted and Bro. E. Middleton of Leigh was elected to fill the vacancy. Under the head of "Good of the order," an earnest and vigorous address was given by Bro. Morris Jones, D.Sec., and Bros. J. W. Roberts, G. Clarke, E. Martin, John Taylor, G. E. Warburton, &c., took part in the dicussion which followed, it being decided to hold a short open air meeting prior to the indoor gathering.—Thanks to Bro. Jones for his address,and to the Vulcan friends for the excellent arrangements they had made, brought a very enjoyable session to a close. A public tea followed, at which a large number were present, at the close an adjournment being made to the " Square," where an open air meeting was held, addresses being given by Bros. Dale and Jones. A meeting was afterwards held in the schoolroom. Bro. Quartermaster-Sergeant Thaberts, of Warrington presided, and he was supported by Bros. M. Jones, G. Clarke, W. H. Dale, G. E. War- burton, W. Blair, E. Martin, R. Simms, &c. Earnest addresses were given by the chairman and Bro. Jones, and an excellent programme of songs, recita- tions, &c., was submitted by. Bros. Roberts, Taylor, Rigby, E. Taylor, Sisters Harrison, Astra Ord, Travis, Cordingley, Mrs. and Miss Nurse (Warring- ton). Votes of thanks to the Chairman and speakers, terminated the meeting.

A SAILOR SERIOUSLT INJURED AT RUNCORN.

A seaman on the schooner Tom Roper, of Lancaster, named Wm. T. Cort on Sunday became entangled in a rope whilst the vessel was entering Runcorn Dock. One of his legs was seriously injured, the flesh being very much torn. He would have sustained further injury but for the assistance of a ship mate who managed to release him. He was attended by Dr. McKenzie and on Monday Messrs. Wm. Shaw (missionary) and Wm. By- conveyed him on an ambulance to the station, Prom wl!ence they went to Liverpool. Here the injured man was lodged in the Royal Southern Hospital, where he is receiving the attention his injuries require.

LECTURE AT RUNCORN ON THE" CATACOMBS OF ROME." Mr. Daniel Bisbrown read a paper on Friday evening on the above subject at the weekly meeting of the Ellesmere-st. Free Church Improvement Class., the chair- man of the gathering being Mr. James Scragg. The essayist described the catacombs roughly as long and narrow subterranean galleries, wherein lay Rome's Christian dead of the early centuries. It is impossible to explore these labyrinths without a guioe. The rash adventurer would be almost certain to find no exit. The entire length of the various passages had been computed by a competent calculator at 587 miles, equal to the .entire length of Italy, and the number of graves, according to the same authority, was not less than 3,831,000. Some have even estimated them as eight millions. After the reading of the paper there was a discussion, in which the following members of the class took part I—Messrs. Edward Gandy, James Turnbull, Wesley Cooke, and Joseph Newall. A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Bisbrown, after which the meeting closed. lIICOLLIER'S sell the best quality goods lat lowest postible prices. —Advt. AN INCORRIGIBLE LAD AT RUNCORN.

We are pleased to be ma Position to state that a change for the better has taken place in the condition of Mr. S. B. Dr. McDougall, of Runcorn, is in constant attendance upon the sufferer, and hopes are now held out that he will speedily recover. FORTRCOMING CONCERT AT RUNCORN. div.head: BODIES
div.p: BODIES

On Monday the bodies of Captain Abrams, Albert-st., Runcorn; and Thomas Jones, Widnes, (mate) were thrown up at Abergele and Llandulas respectively. It will be remembered that on the 21st October the flat " Rose," owned by Messrs. Speakman and Sons, Run- corn, foundered off Penrraen Held, near Colwyn Bay, and that the men named who were in charge of her were drowned whilst endeavouring to get ashore. The bodies were in an advanced state of decomposition. Inquests have been held and verdicts of " Accidentally drowned" have been returned in both cases. The bodies have been brought home, and that of Robert Abrams will be interred in the Runcorn Cemetery this (Friday) afternoon. The deceased captain leaves a widow and one child.
RUNCORN AND THE FORTHCOMING ELECTIONS :-ACTION
BY THE LIBERAL COUNCIL.

The members of the Runcorn Liberal Council met again in the St. John's assembly room, Runcorn, on Fri- day evening under the chairmanship of Mr. A. K. Norman. It will be remembered that a committee was elected at the adjourned meeting for the purpose of pre- paring a report. That report the Committee now sub- mitted, and was in the form of a programme. After being discussed at some length the report was adopted, and the Council decided to send a copy to each candidate and await replies. The meeting then again stood ad- journed. The Council met again on Tuesday evening, when the only business transacted was the election of committees for ths various wards. LOCAL GOVERNMENT INQUIRY AT RIINCMI.N.

On Thursday morning, Colonel Arthur S. Durnford, RE., Inspector appointed by the Local Gpvernment Board,held an inquiry at the Runcorn Town Hall into an application, made by the Runcorn Improvement Com- missioners, under the Technical Instruction and Public Health Acts, for sanction to borrow £2,070. This sum was made up of the following items :—£1,250 for pur- poses of technical instruction ; £5OO for works of sewer- age; £220 for the provision ot a flushing van and urinals to be erected at Doctor's Bridge, Delph Bridge, Waterloo Bridge, and Mersey-str,et and £lOO for pur- poses of street improvement. There were present Messrs. James Pritchard, W. Handley, E. Imison, and F. Wiswall, Commissioners ; Mr. F. A. Lake, law clerk to the Com- missioners • Mr. E. Marshall, secretary ; Mr. Boden, architect of the Institute, and Messrs. N. Barber, sur- veyor, and J. Wilding, assistant surveyor. Particulars of the various loans were given by Mr. Lake and others, and at the termination of the inquiry, the Inspector proceeded to inspect those parts of the town where the improvements were proposed to be made. MIRACULOUS.ESCAYE FROM DEATH NEAR RUNCORN.

On Thursday afternoon, at about half-past four o'clock a paid-off seaman, named John McKnight, of Belfast, but who is temporsrily residing at 103, Percival-lane, met with an accident whilst on board the "Kathadin," then lyicg at Saltport. It appears that McKnight, being anxious to get work went aboard for the purpose of see- ing the secoLd mate. He was told that the mate was aloft, attending to some sails, and forthwith began to climb up to speak to him. He had reached the main yard when by some means he fell. In his descent he struck the rigging, and then the wooden jetty, and from thence was tossed into the Ship Canal, He was quickly picked out of the water and conveyed on board the . fiat Mary, (which was being tugged) to Runcorn. • Dr. Mangan attended the injured man at the latter's lodgings, and found him partly un- conscious. Owing to his condition no examination, to discover the extent of his injuries, was made. Every- thing possible was done for him, and so far as can at present be judged he is progressing as favourably as can be expected. The distance which the man fell was more than seventy feet, and had the fall not been broken by the rigging, he would undoubtedly have been killed. McKnight is about 20 years of age.

PROPOSED CHURCH FOR WESTON. _ _ _

The bazaar to raise funds towards the bui:ding of a proposed new church for Weston, was opened on Wednesday, in the Public Hall, Runcorn. The bazaar was representative of "Runcorn in Ye Olden 'Lyme," at the date, perhaps, of 1670, and we cannot do better, perhaps, than give our readers the descrip- tion of the bazaar as given in the neat little handbook issued by the committee:—" Visitors entering the Public Hall by its first door enjoy a veritable transformation scene. Passing through the staircase vestibule they turn to the rigibt, and after passing the cloak room they enter the old town of Runcorn through the great gate- way of the castle. Right away in front of them—almost untouched by the hand of time—stands We eld Parish Church as it thtn stood, ort. the edge of the river Mer- sey, and surrounded by, well-wooded and beautiful meadows. Prominent in the foreground, is the ancient Lych gate, and somewhat nearer is the old Market Crosse—at which Lady Brootirs will vend her pretty flowers. On either hand solid looking houses line the street. On the right at the sign of "ye Stores" and "ye Old Court Nouse " the ladies from the Parish Church, dressed inCavalier orßound head habit display their wares A little further down at "ye Old Curiosity Shop" the inhabitants of Weston proffer their goods for sale. Right across at "ye Weston Wvnd " another party from the same village invite buyers. Down 44 ye Change Alley" visitors can take a little refreshment at "ye Chesshyre Cheese." Returning by the same way, and still keeping to the right, the ladies from St. Michael's will be pleased to exchange their merchandise for their gold and silver at" ye Mercers' Hall" and "ye Golden Web." A little time may then be spent in viewing the massive walls of the Old Castle, or if more frivolously inclined they may visit the Gipsy Queen in her Wigwam, or crack their sides with laughing at the merry entertainments in the room beyond the church. The town itself is en fete ; everything proclaims this, and the happy faces and bright peculiar costumes will help all to realise it." undermentioned is a list or the stall and stalls h,lders : Parish Church stall : Mesdames Maitland, Wood, Abell, Itnison, Maclennan, Whitaker, and Miss Smith. At the opening cermony on Wednesday afternoon the hall was crowded. The Rev. Canon Wood, dressed in the habit of a Rector of Runcorn in the latter portion of the 17th century, appeared on the platform in the front of the church, and was accompanied by the High Sheriff of Cheshire, Mr. Frederick Harrison. Miss Harrison,Mrs. Maitland Wood, Miss Barclay, Dr. Steele, and Mr. T. T. Sill.

The Rector, who spoke the dialect of the period which his costume represented, introduced the High Sheriff in a most amusing speech. He spoke of the object of the ' bazaar, and said that Major Orred had not only granted , them a plot cf land upon which to erect the sacred edi- fice, but in addition had given them a donation of £lOO towards the building of the same. (Applause.) The total amount ri quired was £2,000. The High Sheff expressed the great pleasure it gave him to open the bazaar which was a very peaceful duty compared with some of the duti(.s the Rector had said that sheriffs generally performed in the olden times. He hoped all of them would set to work and if they worked hard, he might prophesy that before Saturday night arrived they would be in possession of a good round sum, quite enought to warrant the beginning of the erections of the church. (Applause.) No one should leave the bazaar before their pockets;were emptied. He

CHILDREN'S CONCERT AND OPPE RETTA AT E A RLESTO WN.

On Thursday night the Town Hall at Earlestown was packed with an enthusiastic audience on the occasion of a concert and opperetta given by the children attending the Earlestown District School, which is presided over by Mr. A. Brown as head- master, Mrs. Brown officiating as bead mistress. It appears that since the school became a free school, some difficulty has been experienced in meeting the requirements of the Educational department, aris- ing principally from the fact that during the first two years the school was opened, the Department considerably reduced the grants. The expenses being consequently heavier, some means had to be devised to assist the diminished revenue, and it was decided to enlist the assistance of the children to this end. Mr. and Mrs. Brown and the whole of the staff of teachers therefore set to work, to train a selected num- ber of children, and after several weeks of arduous labour, the concert on Thursday night was the result. Childrens concerts are always an acceptable commodity, and are an agreeable change from the performances of more experienced artistes, and although there may occasionally be a few mistakes, yet these are allowed to pass by the audience, when the earnestness and hearti- ness with which the children enter into their task is taken into account. This being the first effort of the kind put forth by Mr. and Mrs. Brown in Earlestown, they are to be congratulated upon the success which attended a first venture, and we do not doubt that they will be stimulated to still further enterprise in the future. The platform of the Town Hall, although capacious enough for any ordinary purpose, had to be still further enlarged, and this is not to be wondered at when accommodation had to he found for about 200 bays and girls, who were arranged in tiers, presenting a pleasing picture, the majority of the girls being robed in white. In addition to the children assistance was rendered by Miss Annie Molyneux, who, though suffering from a cold, sang fairly well "Home, dearie home," and Mrs. Brown who sang "Daddy." We may here state that although the audience was not very demonstrative, they were nevertheless heartily appreciative, and in one instance only 'did they depart from the natural ceol- ness of Earlestown audiences and vouchsafe an encore, hut in this case they simply could not help themselves. To save space it would be as well perhaps to state here that each item was submitted by the children in a most efficient and careful manner' and evidenced the careful training they had received. The item deserving of special mention was the two-part song "Whistle and floe," the boys at the end of each chorus whistling and tne girls humming a refrain. The choral selections were "The old Brigade," "The Vesper Hour," "Sleighing," "Sweet and low," duet " Let us gather bright flowers," Misses A. Bailey, L. Barr, L. Jones, F. Sprcston, and K. Holdsworth, and Master C. Rawlings. Seng, "The Chorister," Master W. Atttield, for a youngster, was excellently submitted. Song, "Little Gypsy Jane," by Miss Lily Barr, with tambourine accompaniment and dance, brought down the house, and she had to repeat the last verse. Musical drills also formed a portion of the entertainment, the girls being in charge of Miss Nash, and the boys of Mr. Stringer, assistant master, and they performed their tasks with remarkable precision. At the interval a number of books were distributed by Captain Ruse, RN., as prizss awarded to successful scholars in the various branches. In making the pre- sentations, he said he was very pll'ased to be there that evening to give away those prizes, as he took a great interest in the school. He had nearly 400 schools in his district, which he visited every year, for drawing, and of these 135 passed excellent, 230 good, and only 30 of them stood fairly well. In Lancashire there were 1,841 day schools and 140 evening, with 277.720 scholars. In Yorkshire there were 2,034 day and 75 evening schools, with 228.797 scholars. In all England and Wales there were 18,438 day and 464 evening schools, with 1.853,008 scholars. Lancashire had one tenth of the number of day schools in England and Wales and one seventh of the scholars taught drawing. The district school was opened as a mixed schseal in 1891, and in 1893 and 4 they attained excellent in every subject. It rrflected very great credit on the management, the teachers, and everybody connected with the schools, to attain such e result in so short a period. Outof the 400 schools,there were many excellent, and that was one of them. (Ap- plause.) -He went to no school where the children were better behaved than at the Earlestown District School. (Applause.) Be then distributed the prizss as under :—Attendance. —Names of children mot absent during the year ended May 31st, 1894 :—Mixed school : Standards V. and VI., William Drummood, Alice Bailey, Charlotte Bailey ; Standard IV., Joseph Smith, David Kinsey, William Savage, Samuel Hatton, Robert Deluce, Ellen Tripp, Jane Boughey, Lily Barr, W. Pickup ; S,andard 111., Fred Hallett, Thomas Pope, Frank Cooper, Thomas Hardie, John Savage, Joseph Green, Georee Bellis, James Dean, Albert Edwards, Robert Barlow, Fred Holt, Ellen Hassell, Kate Stride, Emily Watkinson ; Standard 11., Arthur Pendry, Alfred Eaton, Frank Hulmes, Hannah Tonks ; Standard 1., John Hallett.Fred Pickup, William Hassell, John S:ureess, Arthur Barlow, Annie Stureess, A. Dickenson. Children absent one half-day only: Emily Hughes. Ellen Sturgess, Maude Green, Henry Warburton, Alfred Sturg,ess. Merit :—Standard I.—F. Smith (drawing), M. Tither (arithmetic), J. Bott (reading), W. Walton (geography), R. Smith (mental arithmetic), W. Leatherbarrow (gram- mar), A. Waddington (recitation), M. Millington (writ- ing), S. Fairhust (needlework). Standard IL—E. Spencer (drawine), E. Scott (recitation). M. Appleton (readine), J. Robinson (seography). F. Kenning (arith- metic). L. Rawlings (grammar), J. Ogden (writing), Ed. Ellis (mental arithmetic). M. Baseldine (needle- work). Standard lII.—F. Hallett (arithmetic), M. Sid- deley (writing), T. Muscroft (grammar), C. Jones (recitation), Ernest Barker (mental arithmetic), T. Muscroft (drawing), A. Haseldine (needlework), F. Cooper (reading.), T. Hardie (geography), F. Austen, Standard IV.—A. Cronin (arithmetic), W. Savage (writ- ing), T. Mawdsley (drawing), P. Smith (Needlework), W. Atefield (grammar) K. Hohlsworth (reading), C. Rat- cliffe (recitation) E. Sixmith (mental arithmetic), S. Wright (geography), T. Waring. Standards V. VI., VII.—L. Jones (arithmetic), E. Hilton (arithmetic), A. Green (grammar), A. Adams (Needlework), G. Cooper (composition), G. Holliday (mental arithmetic), C. Raw- lings •(composition), H. Wilson (drawing), T. Lord (geography), E. Lewis (reading), J. Latham (recitation), H. Waddington (drawing). Prizes for special progress, given by Dr. Handyside, obtained by Sarah Balmer aad Robert Deluce. At the conclusion, the second part of the programme, around which perhaps the greatest interest centred,was proceeded with, and was carried through with a success fully meriting all the praise bestowed upon it. This consisted of an operetta, entitled " Fairy Fay." The dramatis persekae, if the phrase may be used, were : King of Gohbins, Master Charles Rawlings ; Queen of Fairies, Miss Maggie Southern ; fairies, Misses F. Ken- ning. J. R. Robinson, E. Eaton, E. Ellison,L, Makeham, M. Naylcr, E. A. Smith. and F. Sutton. Imps, Masters H. Gee, E. Hall, J. Jones, R. Jones, H. Muscroft, H. Waddington, E. Waring, F. Valentine, J. Lowe, W. Parry. Villagers, Misses A. Bailey, L. Eaton, K. Holdsworth, C. Ratcliffe, Masters W. Attfield, F. Banton, E. Smith, S. Wright. The plot or argument was developed in five scenes, and, briefly described, showed that the King of the Goblins sends his Imps to sow diseord amongst certain friends gathered on the village green. A quarrel takes place amongst the villagers, supposed to be caused by the Imps. The Imps return, and are commended by their King for the amount of mischief they have caused. " Fairy Fay" appears on the scene, and sends her Sprites to undo the wrong worked by the Imps. The quarrel of the villagers is made up, and the final is reached by a happy reunion all round, the moril be- ing "The triumph of genial friendship over vicious temper." The Imps were really imps in reality, and fairly revelled in the business allotted to them, their acting and singing and reciting being superb. The King of the Goblins upheld the part in a really clever manner, and we doubt if Mr. Brown could have made a better choice in the whole school than Master Rawlings. The dresses of the Imps were fully characteristic, and being made in the school, did credit to the costumiers. The villagers did their part equally well, and their make-up as country children was clever. The dancing and singing which they indulged in was very effective, and the dialogue was capitally recited, the character of " Sue " deserving special mention. The Fairies upheld their character, and altogether the affair was a decided success, the final chorus being, "What shall we sing at Christmas ?" At the close a vote of thanks was accorded Captain Rnyse, who in responding, secured for the children the next day as a holiday.

Trturr FROM A &Ran. At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday morning Win. Darby (12) was charged with stealing from the Trinity Schools at half-past eleven on Thursday the Bth inst. a boy's overcoat,value 29.—Inspector Spinks said that the complainant was Colin Bloomfield, son of Richard Bloomfield,and attended the Trinity School. On the day in question he hung his coat up in the school vestibule and on coming out he found that it was gone. Informa- tion was given to P.C. Roper and he apprehended the prisoner. When charged with the theft he replied " I took it last Thursday." Mr. Riley said that the boy had been previously expelled from the Trinity school for truancy. His mother, who was present, said that on Thursday night the lad never came home but on Friday he returned with the coat in his possession. He told his mother that a woman had given it him because he looked starved. The magistrates ordered him to receive six strokes with the birch and be detained until 6 o'clock.
