FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Wright (chairman), Coun- cillors Roberts and Pierpoint, Dr. Gornall, and Mr. S.

Wright. ABSCONDING FROM THE WORKHOUSE.—George Chatta- way was sent to gaol for 14 days for absconding from the workhouse on the Bth inst., and refusing to perform the work which he was required to do. THEFT OF A WATCH AND CHAlN.—Percy John Barrett, last from Oakmere, was charged with stealing from the dwelling-house of George Dixon, 11, Bayhorse-yard, on the 7th inst., a silver watch and chain, valued 30s. The evidence was that Mr. and Mrs. Dixon had taken the prisoner in the house, as he was an orphan. They told him about a week afterwards that he ought to be doing something for his keep. He went away the same night, and the watch and chain were then missed. He was afterwards arrested by Detective Monaghan. The watch was found secreted in the closet.—The prisoner pleaded guilty to stealing it.—He was sent to goal for 14 days without hard labour. BREACH or THE FACTORY ACTS.—John Thomas Harri- son, confectioner, Winwick-road, was eummoned at the instance of Mr. James Henry Rogers, Inspector of Factories, that on the 11th October be employed a child named Joseph Caldwell Knox (12) without having a certificate of school attendance from the school- master. Mr. Rogers stated that he visited the defendant's place and found the boy working. No certificate had been obtained as to the boy's attendance at school. The boy had left schoo three months. He should attend school half-time, and it wal the defendant's duty to get a certificate from the headmaster of the school certifying that the boy had done so. No person was allowed to employ a child under 13 under any circumstances in a factory or work- shop rodaer than as half-timer, and it was also a condi- tion that the children being so employed should go to school on the half-days or alternate days. The defendant stated that the boy came to him and said that he had passed the fifth standard. He had no abstract of the Factory Act in his possession, and stated that he did not know the law on the matter. He had been in business four years and was not supplied with the abstract. —The Inspector on being questioned as to how it came about that they had missed visiting the defendant's premises • lorg, stated that the factory inspectors' staff for the district consisted of three men and they had about seven thousand places in the district to visit. They were increasing at the rate of twenty per week. The magistrates imposed a fine of 2s. ed. and costs, • CRIIRI.TY TO ANIMALS.—Wm. Pennington, Orford, was charged with having on the 31st, October,in the borough of Warrington, unlawfully illtreated a horse by working it while in an unfit state.—Inspector Liiff, R S.P.O A, stated that at 12.30 on the date named he was at Market Gate when he saw the defendant driving a ronv which was lame in the near hind leg. It stand still for some time in Buttermarlaet-street and he noticed that it put no weight on that foot. On starting again the pony seemed worse so he stopped it and found that it was suffering from a spavin. The leg was inflamed and very tender. He had cautioned the defendant six weeks previously.—The defendant denied that the horse was in any pain. He was fined ss. and costs.—Joseph Quinn, greengrocer, Warrington, was charged with a similar offence committed on the same day. Insppctor Luff in proving this case said that defendant was the owner of the mare and he saw it attached to a green- grocer's cart in Bridge-street. It was lame in both hind legs. Defendant was fined the same amount as the last offender. P.C. Turner corroborated in both cases. SavanDAY.—Before Islessirs. J. Bergess in the chair), S.

Chandley and 1,. Vo'sev. STRiNeE CONDUCT OF A DRUNKEN MAN,—James B Aldred, gentleman, Leigh Villas, Grapnenhall, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bewsev-st. at half-past six on Friday night.—Mr. Hunt (chief con- stable) stated that the romp!airant was Mrs. Weaver. sister of Mr. Thomas Jones, Bewsev-road, Warrington On the night named complainant was going along Bewsey-at. when the defendant followed her persistontiv till she got near her father's house in Frocylaii.lan,;, where on the door being opened to her knock she fell down exhausted. Her brother,flarry Jones,then went to the defendant and asked him for an explanation, and not ,getting one he gave him into custody.—H. B. Jones said he was the brother of the complainant and corro- borated Mr. Hunt's statement, adding that the man was very drunk.—P.C. Jones deposed to receiving a com- plaint from the last witness and going to his residence and there seeing complainant who appeared very ill.— Mr. Weaver, husband of the complainant, stated that his wife was too ill to appear. and had told him that the defendant had run very fastiv after her for a dis- tance of about 180 yards. Ho did not wish to press case.—Inspector Spinks deposed that he saw the defend- ant brought in and did not think he was responsible for hia actions he was so drunk.—Defendant had told him that he had had some whiskey at a private house and he thought there must have been something in it to effect him so.—He was fined 10s. and oasts. D.RUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Kate Ann Jones was charged pith committing this offence on Friday night on Pinner's Brow. Having a good character of late, she was dismissed. A DETERMINRD YOUNG TiflEF.—Abraham Gerrard (10) was charged with stealing half-a-orown from the bake- house of Stephen Ravenscroft, 3 Rovve-st., on Friday afternoon. The lad had lived with his mother in London where he had stolen a postal order for 255. and with this money had come to Warrington by himself and gone to his aunt's (Mrs. Ravenscroft) and there stolen the half-crown and then gone to Liverpool, where he was apprehended and sent back. It was stated that he had been before the London magistrates for stealing and then dismissed. He was ordered to receive six strokes of the birch-rod.

ALLEGED THEFT OF BOOTS.--William Coyne, Turner-st., was charged with stealing from 3, rurnei-st., on the 6th November, a pair of lace-up boots, value is. 6d. the property Of William Tickle. It appears that defendant lodged at a common lodging-house kept by Mrs. Tickle and on the date named having no shoes of his own he told Mrs. Tickle's daughter that he was going to get a pair out of the yard. She cautioned him about doing so but he took the pair produced. Defendant said he had been wearing the boots a week and Mrs. Tickle knew about it. P.C. F. Cooper deposed to apprehending the defendant. Jane Tickle and her daughter, Ann Tickle, gave evidence as to the defendant taking the boots. The magistrates dismissed the defendant but recorded a con- viction against him. A GAME OF CHANCE.—George Dickenson, 4, Chapel court, John-st., and Gilbert Berry, 37, Scotland-ro ad were both charged with playing a game of chance with cards in Bewsey-st. on the 4th Nvoember. Both pleaded guilty. P.C. Bell s..id that he saw defendants playing with cards for money under the Bewsey-st. railway arches on the date named. Both defendants were ordered to be detained two days. L' CRUELTY TO A MARE.—Joseph Lawrenson, market r gardener, Old-road, was charged with cruelly ilitreating a horse by working it while in an unfit state on the 27th October last.—lnspector Luff, R.S.P.C.A. stated that shortly before 11 o'clock on the night of the 27th of October he was in the Market Place when he saw a bay gelding drawing a cart of vegetables. It was lame in the off fore leg and in pain. He had it taken out of the shafts and the following morning he saw it in the stable and found that it was suffering from an injury to the foot caused some time before, The defendant had been compelled to bring this animal out because his other horse had hurt its knees. The inspector did not wish to press the case. Defendant was dismissed on payment of the costs. TUESDAY. —Before Dr. Gornall (in the chair), and Dr. T Starkey Smith. A WARNING TO TRUANTS.—On the application of Mr. G. Riley, school attendance inspector, Edward Thorni- croft (12), son of Edward Thornicroft, forgeman,Wake- ' field-st., was sent to the training ship Clio, for truancy. WRDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough.(chairman),

Mr. J. Geddes, and Mr. j. H. Fleming. A SERIOUS OFFENCE.—George Lowe, an elderly man, was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart in Bridge-street at half-past two on Tues- day afternoon. Defendant pleaded guilty.—P.C. Bruen said that at the time named he saw the defendant in charge of a horse and cart loaded with coal. He was sitt- ing among the coal and incapable of holding the reins. Witness btopped the cart, and with the assistance of P.C. Hardy they got him off and brought him to the police station.—Mr. Hunt stated that he had known the defendant 30 years and he had always been a steady, honest man. This was his first appearance in court.— He was fined 53. and costs. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Wm. Noon for being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street at 10.40 on Tuesday sight was fined ss. and costs. A similar penalty was in- flicted on Lawrence Deane for being drunk in Dallam- lane, on Wednesday morning. THURSDAY.—Before the:Mayor (Councillor James Fair dough) in the chair, Alderman Sutton and Major

Ridgway. IEMPORART ALITHORITY.-I.emporary authority was granted to John Hughes to sell at the Wheat Sheaf. To George Grounds to sell at the Volunteer, Cockhedge. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—The following people were dean with for not sending their children to school. Mr. G. Riley. prosecuted: Eli Jevons, forgeman, Eliza- beth-st., 2s. 6d.; John Dutton. labourer, Silver Square; 2s. 6d.: Charles Roberts, hawkar, Haydock•st., 23. 6d. John Mackie, forgeman, Winwick-road, ss.
NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS. SATURDAY.—Before Mr, T. J. Gillespie (chairman),and

Colonel J. L. Wood. DRUNEENNESS.—For this offence the following were fined: John Parker, Newton, ss. and costs; Samuel Walton, Newton, Es. 6d. and costs: William Foster, Winwick, 2s. 6d. and costa; Patrick Ryan, Newton. ss. and costs; Patrick Flaherty, Newton, 2s. 6d. and costs; Henry Jones, Flaydock, 53. and costs; James Ashall, Haydock, 2s. Ed. and costs. DOGS AT LARGE.—For allowing their dogs to be at large, Annie Fazaekerly, Newton, was fined 7s. 61.; Elizabeth Rhodes, Newton,7B. 6d.;Blandina or Margaret Francis, Newton, 7s. Bd. IRREGULAR ATTENDANCE AT SCHOOL.—William Done, Golberne, was fined ss. for neglecting to send his child regularly to school. Mr. Henry Pegg prosecuted. A NEGLECTFUL PARENT.—Thomas Johnson, Gol borne, was charged with neglecting his children on October 5, and divers other duties and thus causing them unneces- sary suffering. Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor, who pro- secuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C. said that the de- fendant and his wife and daughter had been summoned for the same offence on the previous sessions. The wife and daughter had been dealt with, but the husband did not then appear. He had since given himself up to the police. The defendant laid the blame of the neglect upon his wife, as he gave her his money every week. He earned 30s. per week, and a boy earned 7s. per week, so that poverty was no reason why snch a state should exist.—lnspector McAteer then recapitulated the evid- ence given last sessions against the wife and daughter, and which was fully reported in our columns at the time. The defendant said that he was a hard-working man, and del all he could for his children. If he spoke to his wife about them she only called him "bad names.' After a short consideration, Mr. Gillespie in announcing the decision of the bench said that he had no dout but that the defendant was under the thumb of his wife, but he ought to have reported the state of his children to the proper authorities, and he would therefore he fined 20s. and cots, or 14 days imprisonment in default. ALLEGED UNLAWFUL WOUNDING —William Green wood, Golhorne, was charged with unlawfully wounding James Melling, Golborne on November 4th. Mr. Stuart defended. It was alleged that Greenwood had broken Mellings 1e while being being ejected from the Marian Arms, while the defence was that it was caused by a fall. Melling was unable to appear, and the case was adjourned until the next clay, hail being allowed.

fiflr"lr RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.• MONDAY.—Before Messrs. Philip Speakman, C.C.. lr. J. Norman, and S. Taylor. DOG OWNERS IN TROUBLE —Elizabeth Malkin ,Weston Point ; Charles Whitley, 40, Shaw-street ; and Nathaniel Harding, Frodsham ; were each ordered to pay costs for allowing their dogs to wander at large unmuzzled. SUSPENSION OF THE MUZZLING ORDER. —The Chair- man (Mr. Speakman) intimated that the order issmed by the County Council,relating to the muzzling of dogs, had now been suspended. This, however, it must be borne in mind, did not interfere with the obligation resting upon owners to see that their dogs wore collars bearing their names and addresses. Dugs would have to wear properly addressed collars, just the same as before.—Superintendent Atherton said that the neces- sary notices had been posted up that morning. IRREGULAR ATTENDANCE AT SCHOOL.—Wiltiam Webster, Greek-street ; Henry Snape, Gilbert-street ; Henry White, Princess-street ; and John Rourke, Fryer-street; were each fined 61. and 4a. 61. costs for not sending their children regularly to school. DAMAGING THE RAILWAY COMPANY'S PREMISES. —John Shingler,Greenway-rood, was charged with having done damage amounting to 55., to a window on the premises of the London and North-Western Railway on the pre- vious Saturday night.—lsaac Walls, a porter in the em- plcv of the comnany named, said that whilst he was on duty at the railway station on the night of the 10th inst., between the hours of eleven and twelve, the pris- oner began to quarrel with a man and woman near the ticket collector's office. He attempted to knock the man down and thrust his fist through a pane of glass into the office. Subsequently when the prisoner was outside he struck the female.—Sliperintendent Atherton remarked that when apprehended on Sunday morning, prisoner was under the influence of drink.—The prisoner who pleaded that the window was broken purely by accident, was fined 6d. and 63. 4d. costs, and also the damage, 53.

RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. WIDNES.

When the Warrington team accompanied by a large number of their supporters steamed out of the Central Station on Saturday afternoon for the well-known chemical town of Widnes, there was not only a prospect ot a fine afternoon but an evenly contested match. The latter of these anticipations was realised but the weather was unfavourable. For a short time prior to the kick-off there was a heavy shower of rain and again just before the first half of the game had been completed rain fell plentifully, and continued until the game was almost completed. This soddened the ground and drenched the players but they stuck to their task doggedly and good- humouredly despite the unfavourable elements. At the Widnes v. Warrington matches a good deal of rivalry has existed and some unseemly behaviour has been wit- nessed. But on Saturday no -fault with the players, or spectators, could be found, and a most pleasant and interesting game, although somewhat spoilt by the rain, was the result. The busy prophets had predicted that Widnes would win and the Warrington team was not one to be over sanguine about seeing that there were no fewer than five players who belonged to the " A " team. When the referee (Mr. J. C. Seddon) gave the signal for the commencement of the match the following composed the respective teams : Warrington : full back, Boscow ; threequarter backs, Cunningham, Heesom, Burton and Mores; half-backs, Bate and Foden ; forwards, Turner. Thorniley, Berry, Taylor, Andrews, Buckley, Bsiley,and Savage. Widnes, full back, Brennan ; thmequarter backs, Alford, Rispan, Nevitt, and Clark ; half-backs, Drummond and Barber ; forwards, Hogan, Whelan, Johnson, Fraser, Emery, Derbyshire, King and Grace. Burton commenced operations against the wind and with a huge kick sent the ball well into the home quarters. Rispan for Widnes failed to respond to the kick and the Warrington forwards rushing up took the ball to the Widnes line and were unlucky in not voring at the very outset of the game. Clark pluckily saved his side from disasteriand after a few scrimmages had taken place Widnes came away with a rush, transferring play

to Warrington territory, and causing Burton to save. The home team were shortly afterwards awarded a penalty kick in a good position for scoring, but Barber failed at the kick. The drop out did not bring much relief for Warrington, for the Widnesians pressed for- ward,and were only stayed from scoring by Boscow,Bate, Moores and Burton being smart in saving. Cunningham was nest conspicuous in bringing relief to his side by a run past the half way flag, but the home tam from the ensuing scrimmage again called upon Boscow to save. A penalty kick,for off side play, helped Warring- ton a little, and Moores brought further relief to his side by a short run and kick. The home team now forced two minors by long kicks. Drummond essayed a drop at goal, but without any tangible result. A fine rush by the Warrington forwards, Berry, Thorniley, Savage, and Andrews being prominent, now took play near the Widnes line. From the scrimmage Bate almost got ever the line. A number of scrimmages took place and eventually Bate made his mark, giving Warrring- ton a free kick in an advantageous position. Burton took the kick, but was unsuccessful, the ball just going outside the posts. Warrington continued to press for some time after the drop out, until Widnes were awarded a penalty kick which they made good use of. Foden was applauded for a tricky run, but Barber col- lared him when near the Widnes line. Cunninghaws was soon afterwards unlucky in not crossing the Widnes line, being brought down to "mother earth" when within a few feet from the line. Widnes again carried _ .

play out of danger with a strong rush, and the visitors had some difficulty in staying their progress. Another penalty kick was awarded Widnes, hut little advantage was gained by it. Nevitt accidentally received a kick on the ankle, and play was stopped for a short time. Rain began to fall, and give and take play followed until half time time arrived, with a clean sheet. On the restart Widnes commenced to attack but Boscow defended admirably. A good rush headed by Berry placed Widnes on the defensive and ahother rush shortly afterwards by the Warrington forwards brought play near the Widnes line. Brennan saved pluckily for his side, and Barber and Drummond were instrumental in taking the play to the half-way flag. A fine passing movement by Foden,Bate, Burton, Heesom and Cunningham was next noticeable and was the means of again taking the venue to the Widnes line. The home defence was impregnable and again did they take the ball out of danger. Burton now made a capital run, and after passing almost all opposition, slipped down near the line. Warrington penned the homesters in their own territory for some time but were only able to score minor points. The last stages of the game were more in favour of Widnes, play for some time resting near the Warrington line. Excite- ment amongst the, spectators now ran high but the defence of Warrington was good and they gradually brought the ball out of danger. Burton taking a conspicuous part. The whistle soon afterwards sounded, the match resulting in a draw, neither side having scored.
WARRINGTON Sr. MARY'S V. PEMBERTON RECS

The return match with the Wigan Junior cupholders was played at Warrington on Saturday, before a good attendance. Pemberton won the toss, and elected to play with the wind, and Hill commenced hostilities for the Saints. After a series of scrimmages at half-way, Pemberton transferred play to the home lines, and Roughley cleared in grand style. A free kick was awarded to Talimer for some off-side play, but was charged down by the Sa'nts' forwards. A round of pass- ing by the home backs followed, and a good chance was missed by Rutter failing to take the pass. From a scrimmage in the visitors' 25, Higginbottom secured and passed to O'Brien. who scored amidst cheers, Hill fail- ing to convert. From the drop-out the game was hotly contested, and midfield was the scene of operations un- til Pemberton got away, only to see Roughley quite safe. Nothing of importance occurred until half-time, when Saints were leading by one try to nil. After the open- ing exchanges the Saints at once pressed, and were in the visitors' quarters in a trice, but were repulsed by Ashton. Eventually Rutter got away, and after a bril- liant run was pulled up by Blackburn on the line. Another rush by the Saints' forwards forzed Sherry to I kick dead. A free kick was awarded to the homesters. Galley returned well, and a fine dribble resulted in Monks scoring. Hill again failed. Immediately after Burrows registered the fourth try, Hampson landing a goal. Resuming, Ashton made his mark in a favourable position, and succeeded in kicking a goal, and when the whistle sounded the Saints ran out by one goal three tries (14 points) to one penalty goal. homesters now pressed, and shortly before time was called Jewkes scored, the final score being Chester College,_ five goals ; Warrington, three goals. ST. MARY'S (WARRINGTON) V. ORFORD.—This match was played at Orford on Saturday, and resulted in a win for St. Mary's. Orford started, and the hornesters several times bccarne dangerous, but the visitors played a good game, and at the interval the score stood—St. Mary's, two goals; Orford, one goal. The second half was not very favourable for football, St. Mary's having to face the rain and a strong wind, and the homesters several times nearly scoredut the backs played a good game and managed to keep them from scoring. St. Mary's now had a chance, and J. S. Richardson scored the third goal for the visitors, and at call of time the score stood St. Mary's three, Orford one. PENKETH RHCREATION V. BRICK-STREET WANDERERS. —This match was played on the ground of the former, on Saturday. Penketh won the toss, and played up hill, with the wino. White started the ball for the visitors, who were soon in the home quarters, but B. Singleton cleared well. Then the Penketh team got away, and F. Singleton scored the first goal. After this the visitors pressed hard, and from a rush White equal- ized. This roused the home team, who began to press, but the defence was good, and play .was in midfield. Some faulty play by the visitors' halves caused Singleton to gain, and he passod out to Foster, and he to Ireland, who made a good run and placed a centre. Then Single- ton scored a second. After this the play was of a one- sided character until the whistle souraded, and the home team ran out victors by nine goals to one. HOWLEY WANDERERS T. BEWSEY ROVERS.—At Bewsey. , Final, Howley 2 goals ; Bewsey 1 goal. WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL V. ASTON HALL.— Played on the ground of the former and after a fast game, victory remained with Aston by 2 goals to 1. Jones and Timmins scored for the winners. WARRINGTON ST. ELPHIN'S V. BLACKBURN ETRURIANS. —That famous Lancashire Amateur Club. the Black • burn Etrurians, paid their first visit to Warrington ~a Saturday to engage in a friendly match with St. Elphins. Both teams were strongly represented, E. E. Wynn- Williams, of Oxford University, making his first appear- ance as left full back for St. Elphin's. The home left took up the running, and from a fine pass by Colley, Hickinbottom beat A. Brier's with a good shot. J.Mercer re-started. The visitors infused a little more vigour into their play, with the result that Pearson and R. Mercer each had ineffective shies, the latter player striking the upright. The Etrurians. forward play was very neat, Barr sending in a shot which brought Robson to the ground, and after some midfield play R. Mercer scored for the Etrurians with a shot which completely beat Rob- son. Hatton at length broke away, and after a pretty run Dendy forced a corner off Carmichael, which Tickell beautifully placed in goal mouth,Colley heading through. The visitors were now having much the best of matters, HiCkinbottom, however, at length broke away,and after , a pretty run transferred to Colley, who shot wide. Play I for a while was in neutral territory, Taylor beautifully tricked Parker,and after a brief breakaway by the home team, Hatton forced a corner, which was well placed. Half time arriving with the score St. Elphin's three goals Blackburn Etrurians two goals. The home team re- started, but the Etrurians were now holding their own, and subjected the home defence in severe ordeal, which they successfully battled against, Forbes eventually re- lieving the tension by pressing the game to neutral terri- tory. Radford was pulled up for off-side, the visitors scoring from the free kick. There was some effective passing between the visitors' forwards, Parker sending in a grand shot, which Robson saved finely, and during the last few minutes of play, the home goal had several escapes. Final result : St. Elphin's, three goals; Black- burn Etrurians, three goals. ST. PAUL'S RESERVE V. HOLY TRINITY RESERVE.—This match was played on the ground of the former. The visitors winning the toss resolved to play with the wind and full time arrived with St. Paul's, one goal; Holy Trinity, nil. PARR VICTORIA V: WARRINOTON L. h N.W. ALBION.— The return match between the above teams took place at Tarr on Saturday last. Losing he toss the Vies kicked off, and at once began to press, but were not allowed to shoot, and the Albions getting the ball they in turn pressed, after which the Vies had slightly the best of matters up to the interval which arrived with Parr 0, Albions 0. Restarting the Albions pressed, but were soon driven back, but it was not until another seven minutes from thee that Parr, with another combined effort rushed a goal. The Albions tried hard to get on an equal footing but were unsuccessful, and the whistle blew with Parr pressing. Final, Parr Vies 1, L. & N.-W. Albions 0. LYNN GRAMMAR Smoot, V. HULME GRAMMAR SCHOOL. —At Lymm on Saturday. A fast game resulted in a victory for the home team by two goals to none. The points were scored by Farrington minor, and Deane. LYNN RESERVE V. WARRINGTON ST. PAUL'S.—At Lymm. A good game resulted in a win for the home team by four goals to one. HOLY TRINITY V. WARRINGTON STAR.—This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday last in very unfavourable weather. At half time the score was in favour of Trinity by 1 goal to nil. On restart- ing the visitors again pressed hard and were not long in Putting in three more goals. At the call of time the score being Holy Trinity 4 goals, Warrington Star nil,

ORFORD CRESCENT T. WIDNES PARISH CHIJRCH.—This match was played on the ground of the former at Orford Lane or. Saturday last, the Parish Church kicking down hill with the wind. From a good bit of passing the Crescent rushed up field to goal mouth, but could not get ball through, the Parish backs clearing to their for- wards whr. got hall away and scored a well earned goal. It was not for long, however, that they had to lead, as a fine hit of passing between Turner, Norman an Weston resulted in the second-named scoring a splendid goal, thus equalising the score at half-time by 1 goal each. Reversing sides the Crescent kicked off with the wind in their favour, and F. Norman got the ball and shot a splendid goal from 25 flag, thus giving the Crescent the lead by 1 goal. Norman scored his third goal from a good bit of passing with him and Turner. Play became very quick and the visitors played up splendidly, the forwards running the length of field an scorin7 a second goal. A very evenly contested game ended in Cres- cent's favour by 3 goals to 2. Parlestown Victoria Rarnton Albion *Newton-le-Willows Parr Victoria Farn wort h C. R.T.S. Connor appeared in the ranks of the homesters for the first time this season. Warrington kicked off, and immediately took the ball to the home quarters, where play rested for a while, the visiting backs having their work cut out to clear their lines. Connor and T.lfather took the ball back, but the visitors would not be denied, and from a scrimmage 'Catesby scored. Chester again broke away and missed two easy chances. The visitors still kept the home defence busy, and after hitting the post, Haynes with a good shot scored. Half-time arrived with the score two goals to nil in favour of the visitors. ST. JOHN'S MISSION HALL.

In aid of the funds of above, an entertainment was given in the liission Hall, on Monday evening, by several of the teachers of St. John's Sunday School and members of the church choir, aided by the Reformatory brass band. There was not a very large audience, but the artistes did their utmost to please, and their efforts met with due appreciation, The Reformatory band were in charge of Mr. J. Dig,weecl (superintendent) and the items, which they submitted was given in a satisfactory manner and fully applauded. An amusing dialogue was also given by several of the teachers, entitled "Bobby's Courtship," the various characters being ably and efficiently sustained. THE MAYOR AT CHURCH.

On Sunday morning in accordance with the usual custom, the new Mayor (Councillor James Fairclough), attended divine service at the War- rington Parish Church,in company with his fellow- members of the Town Council and Corporation offi- cials. The morning was very showery, and the Mayor had provided a number of 'buses to convey the party to church, but it was decided to proceed on foot, as there was a brief spell of sunshine at ten o'clock. The following gentlemen were in the pro- cession :—The Mayor, who had on his left his chap- lain (the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton) and on his right Aid. Francomb (the Duputy-Mayor, Alderman Greenall hav- ing driven to church), Aldermen Sutton, Wright, and Hutchinson : Councillors Baird, Woods, Davies, flep- herd, Hill, Beaman, Longton, Pierpoint, Evans. Shill- cock, Shaw Green, Plumpton, John Lee, Heaton. Smet- hurst, Bennett, and R. T. Fairclough ; Messrs. J. Fair- hurst (borough treasurer), Stanley Wilson (deputy town clerk), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), W.H. Woodcock (assistant borough treasurer), George F. F. White (de- puty clerk to the magistrates), John Sutcliffe (assistant borough surveyor),Qr.Gornall (medical officer of health), Elijah Place (market inspector), R Young (cemetery registrar), W. S. Haddock (gas engineer), Fred Taylor (secretary to the Gas Committee) ; Major Pickmere,J.P., Messrs. John Fairelough, J.P., Thomas Birchall, J.P., James Bolton (one of the borough auditors), Thomas Birtles, J.W Hayward, J.P., and H. Toft, and Messrs. E. Aukland and Alfred Jolley as representing the Board of Guardians. At the head of the procession was the Borough Band, which played suitable selections of music, and thPv were followed by the police under the command of Mr. S. Hunt, the Chief Constable. Next came the fire brigade under the direction of Superinten- dent Turner, and these were followed by the gentlemen mentioned above. There was a large congregation at churoli, anti the clergy present were the Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis), the Revs. G. B. Thurston and H.R.M. Hutt (curates) • the Rev. E. J. Willcocks, and the preacher (the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton). Mr. W.S.Woods presided at the organ. THE SERMON.

The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton took as his text Romans 13c. lv. "Let every soul be subject unto .the higher powers. For there is no power but of God ; the powers that be ordained of God." tie said that religion taught them that the authority of God himself was reflected upon those who were called upon to govern in temporal affairs, and it therefore taught respect for the laws which they administered as a religious duty. It taught respect for the governors et the country whether as magistrates, justices, or legislators, local or imperial, and it gave their authority a divine sanction, and in- ve,ted even their persons with a sanctity, which should dispose all people willingly to submit to their authority. It was therefore policy for any ruler to be disposed favourably to religion, as it taught the people respect for the laws, and submission to authority. They would observe that St. Paul claimed divine authority for the rulers. At that time, the Emperor Nero was upon the throne. Nero was a monster of wickedness and cruelty, and vet St. Paul did not give any countenance for a moment to the fighting against the "higher powers." The people of the present day had undoubtedly a great deal to say about the exercise of authority in all civil affairs. To them belonged the duty of saving which person or persons should have authority, and to whom the government was to be entrusted. But they must not for a moment suppose that that power came from the people simply. They were simply the medium through which the power was given, and net the source. Let them take a corporate body, or representatives in Parlia- ment. They could not take the power of that body until its time of office expired. He contended that that power was ordained from God Himself. It was there- fore necessary in the administration of the country, to look for men of high character, honourable in their deal- ings, and impartial in their judgment, who would fulfil the true interests of the people, while not subservient to their will.
After the service, the procession was re-formed, and marched back to the Town Hall. A large number of people lined the streets the whole length of the route.

div.head: DIED STANDING ON HIS FEET.
div.p: DIED STANDING ON HIS FEET.

"About an hour before sunset last evening, Mary Gunsoly, a servant in the employ of John Roach, a farmer living near Searsville, started out to drive up the cows. She had gone but a short distance along the road when she saw a man standing up against the stone wall, or fence. The perfect quiet which he main- tained, with the ghastly pallor of his face, attracted the woman's attention, and on closer observation she war horrified to find that he was dead. "She at once gave the alarm. The neighbours as- sembled, carried the body to a house near by, and sum- moned Dr. Condict, who pronounced life extinct. The name of the dead man was Patrick Burke ; he was 30 years of age. It is supposed that he was taken 9ud- denly ill while passing along the road ; that he leaned against the wall and died instantly, his body being sup- ported in an erect position by the wall. After the in- quest the coroner's jury rendered a verdict of death by heart failure superinduced by gastritis, or catarrh of the stomach—an acute form of dyspepsia."

The foregoing is quoted from the Middletown "Argus" of November 4th, 1892—an American newspaper. Now let us see what lessons the untimely demise of poor Pat Burke has for some other people who, no doubt, fancy themselves safe from such a sudden tak- ing off. Mr. Thomas Hatt, of Widmere End, High Wycombe, Bucks, was a healthy enough man up to April, 1886. Then he began to weaken and fail. Why he should be ill he couldn't conjecture. So far as he could remember he had done nothing to bring it on. He felt surprised, as a man does at receiving an unexpected blow from behind. His nerves were all of a jangle, be had a bad taste in the mouth, and a sort of all-gone sensation as though the very life were ebbing out of him. His bands and feet were cold and clatnmy, and be often broke out into cold sweats. Dark spots were all the time floating before his eyes, his appetite left him, and when he did eat anything it lay upon him heavy and dull, and seemed to cause a gnawing, grinding pain. " After a time," says Mr. Hatt," I had pain and pal_ pitation at the heart, which I was told was heart dis. ease. At night my heart would thump so hard I could get no sleep ;it sounded like amuftled drum. After a while the heart trouble got so bad I was afraid to yo to bed, and used to sit up nearly all night long. Later on I became so melancholy and nervous that I trembled from head to foot as I went about. I worked a little when I was able, but was always in pain. A doctor in Frog- moor Gardens treated me for somettime, but gave me no relief. I thought I might din any day, for I looked upon my complaint as heart disease. I seemed to be walking in darkness on a narrow footpath between life and death.

"Yet the days, weeks, and months dragged by; I could only wait. It was in October, 1886, that I first read of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. I can't say I I had any faith in it, but there was so much reason and sense in the published accounts of what it had done,that I got a bottle from Messrs. Lansdale and Co., Chemists, Queen's-square, and began to use it. Expecting little or nothing, I received much, for in two days I felt the welcome relief, and after having taken three bottles I found myself in good health ; and have been so ever since—that is, for six years. You are at liberty to publish this letter if you think it might be useful to others, and I shall be glad to answer inquiries. lam a chairmaker by trade, and in the employ of Mr. Gibson Slater-street, High Wycombe. Yours truly (signed) Thomas Hatt, November 15th, 1892."

. Well, you say, how does poor Pat Burke's case connect with Mr. Hatt's ? That's what we are going to tell you. The inquest showed that Burke had no organic disease ef the heart at all. When the doctors cut the heart out of his body they could find no signs of disease about it. What killed him so quickly then ? Listen and learn. The heart derives its motion from the same set of 1-lerves (the pneurnogastric) that move the stomach and lungs. These nerves, poisoned and paralysed by the acids bred by indigestion and dyspepsia, ceased at last to have powar over the heart. Then what? It collapsed in a minute, and the man died before he had time even to lie down on the ground. What a terrible thing! Yet everybody is liable to a like fate who doesn't watch out against indigestion. We congratulate Mr. Hatt on his escape. But it was long odds against him at one time.

THE CRESSWELL BROOK NUISANCE.—On Tuesday, at the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority held in the Workhouse, Dutton, under the chairmanship of Mr. John Mclntyre, Mr. J. div.head: FOREIGN MISSIONARY ANNIVERSARIES AT 'WARRINGTON.
div.p: FOREIGN MISSIONARY ANNIVERSARIES AT 'WARRINGTON.

At Wycliffe Congregational Church, on Sunday, the foreign missionary sermons on behalf of the London Missionary Society, were preached. At the morning service the preacher was the Rev. J. Yonge who, referring to the London Missionary Society, said the present was an interesting period in the history of the Society. Just 100 years ago, on the 4th November, 1794. eight ministers of the gospel met together in a coffee-house in London and commenced the Society. Two of those present were clergymen of the Church of England, two Presbyterians and four Con- gregationalists, and they met as the result of a striking, earnest appeal which had been sent out by Dr. Bogue, Congregationalist minister, of Gosport. They were now approaching a time which was of the deepest interest and which called upon them for renewed exertions in the missionary cause. But when the, only impulse surely was to press on to new developments and to enter upon the second century with renewed effort they were seriously stopped by great financial difficulties. It was more than possible that the existing crisis had come, not entirely from commercial depression, but,it seemed, that among many christian people there was a coldness in the cause of foreign missions. Let them consider a few facts. It had been estimated that the population of of the world amounted to 1,470,000,000. Of this vast population there were 135 millions protestants, 85 millions connected with the Greek church, 195 millions Roman Catholics, 8 minions Jews, and 173 millions Mohammedans, making a total of 596 millions. Thus there were in the 19th century 847 millions of people, pagans, exclusive of 173 millions of Mohammedans who were very little better. Was not that a loud call P Yet there were only 65 thousand protestant missionaries, that number including male and female and wives of missionaries. In proportion to the population in this country there was one preacher of the gospel to every 900 individuals,whereas in India there was one preacher to 168,000 individuals, in Africa one to 222,000, and in China one to 437,000. The rev, gentleman proceeded to speak of the good work accomplished by the London Missbnary Society despite countless difficulties, and appealed for sympathy and help in missionary enter- prise. . . . . . .

- An address to teachers and Sunday school scholars was delivered in Wycliffe schoolroom in the afternoon by the Rev.J. Richardson, missionary for 25 years in Mada- gascar. He also preached to a large congregation in the evening, and spoke of the success which had attended missionary work in Madagascar. The choir effectively rendered an anthem, Mr. W. H. Wallington taking the solo part. Collections were taken at all the services on behalf of the London Missionary Society,

CONCERT AT NEWFIELD INSTITIITE.—On Saturday one I of the series of penny concerts was held in the Newfield Institute. The programme had been prepared by Mr. I Dodds, and all the artistes came from Warrington. The I first part of the programme was commenced by Mr. W. A. Wood giving a pianoforte solo, " Tarantelle." Mr. Frederick Fieldhouse sang "The Wandering Minstrel" in good style, and Mr. A. Grounds greatly amused the nuctience with a humorous musical sketch, "The Silver Wedding." Mr. R. H. Pearson and Mr. W. A. Wood were loudly cheered for a grand trio (violin and piano), " William Tell," and Mrs. R. H. Pearson was very suc- cessful in her rendering of ";The Star of Bethlehem" Mr. Abdey brought the first part to a close with the song "The Message." The second part of the programme was given by the same artistes, who acquitted them- selves wtth great ability. Miss Grounds and Messrs. W. A. Wood and W. H. Payton acted as accompanists. THE LATE MR. LISTER, J.P.—Before commencing the business at the Sale Petty Sessions on Monday, the Chairman of the Bench, Mr. R. H. Joynson, said that he wished to express his own feelings and the feelings of his brother magistrates on the very great loss that they had sustained by the death of Mr. Lister. It was only about ten years since Mr. Lister joined the bench, but he did not think there was any or very few magistrates in Cheshire who could say they had done as much work in ten years as he had done for the county of Chester. Yet in spite of all this work such was the kindliness of Mr. Lister's nature that he always seemed to have a listening ear and an open hand to help anyone who came to him who was in trouble. His loss would not only be felt in Lymm and Altrincham, but in the whole county of Chester, and he by his death had left empty a place which would be exceedingly difficult to fill.—Mr. George Rooke en4orsed the remarks of the Chairman and related a circumstance showing his great consideration for the prisoners who were brought before the court at Lymm and Altrincham.

MISSIONARY SERVICES.—The annual missionary ser- vices were held in the Congregational Church on Sun- day. The Rev. J. Richardson officiated in the morning, and the Rev. Mr. Simpson, of Runcorn, in the evening. There was a good congregation at each service. At the evening service the choir rendered the anthem "0 wor- ship the Lord." Mr. Leather presided at the organ.—On Monday evening the first entertainment of the season in connection with the Band of Hope was held. Songs, recitations Sze.? were given by the following :—The Misses Katie Rowles, F. Brearley, Rose Statham Bertha Spaniel, Sarah Taylor, E. Bradburn, Eva Statham, E. Hinton, A. Barton, Vanda Bennett, M. Brookes, L. Tay- lor, E. Hughes, and Messrs. T. Walker, J. Nicholson, Harold Thornicroft, A. Astley, and Oliver Guest. Dia- logues were also given by several little boys and girls.

div.head: Letter to Mt Otittor.
div.p: Letter to Mt Otittor.

COUNCILLOR SHAW'S A—POLOGY. Sir,—l think it only right that the public of Warring- ton should know the true facts of the case regarding my- self and Councillor Henry Roberts, after the unmanly way he treated my apology. At the advice of my solici- tor I tendered an apology to tha satisfaction of himself and paid costs, therefore thinking I was acting with a gentleman in Councillor Roberts and that here the matter would end, with a public apology. But to my surprise I find it has been cried by every newsboy in the street,through Councillor Roberts having taken it to court without even hinting such a course was to be taken. No apology from me would have been given, but the reverse; I should have fought him in open .court and let the magistrates decide with unbiassed minds. I know who would have come off best. Although aa assault was admitted, the provocation was of such a character that no Englishman could restrain himself from committing it ; for is it not a character a man will defend, and when it is touched by such a man as Councillor Roberts, or any other man, will he not challenge the offender. My opinion about him is that under all the circumstances he might and should have taken a more gentlemanly course.—Yours truly, W. J. SHAW. 89, Dallam-lane.

div.head: FOREIGN COMPETITION IN THE IRON TRADE.
div.p: FOREIGN COMPETITION IN THE IRON TRADE.

Sir,—We are afraid the resolution passed at the meet lag of the Iron Trade Association in Glasgow at the sug- gestion of Mr. Carson may convey a wrong impression to the trade. As far as we know, there is not the slightest iatention on the part of the employers to ask for any reduction of the present wages basis. For some time past, we have felt a falling-off in the export demand for bar and hoop iron, and have naturally sought for the cause. Is the result of our inquiries, extending over a long time, and covering a large area, both at home and -abroad, we have acquired a good deal of information, which, we think, will help to clear the question from any Enisconception as to the real cause of the falling-off in the demand. That it is a very serious matter to the iron trade no one will deny, and none will feel it more than the work- men themselves, and unless they show a greater willing- ' ness than at present to abandon old methods and prejudices, and cheerfully and willingly adapt them- selves to the now posit:on, they will have to face a demand for lower wages, in addition to a lessened de- mand for their labour. After a very careful examina- tion of the whole question we do not despair of being able to hold our own against Belgian manufacturers, providing the workmen will throw themselves as heartily into the solution of the difficulty as we are prepared to do, and give as thoughtful and attentive consideration to his work as the Belgian workman is doing at the present moment. There is no question of royalty as affecting this branch of the bar iron trade, and War- rington is at no disadvantage as regards railway rates to the port. As to shipping freights, we believe that these will be overcome to the extent that English makers will get the same rates as from the Continental ports, and we further say, based upon a thorough know- ledge of the facts, that English makers are at no dis- advantage with their Continental rivals in the cost of the r a vc, material. The whole difference arisns in the cost of labour and greater willingness of their workmen to do what is re- quired to meet the new conditions of manufacture. We say frankly, it is a question almost entirely in the hands of the workmen themselves whether any reduction in wages will be necessary, and it will be time enough to talk about resisting any reduction in wages, when such a proposition is made to alt'r the present wages basis, If tho employers abstain from asking for a reduction -until they have fairly tried what can be done, they have at least a right to expect that workmen will heartily 4nd willingly assist them in every way they can. As regards the manufacture of hoop iron and wire, • the case is somewhat different. America is now taking -the load in both these productions, and at this moment is underselling both the English and German manufac-

turers. In 1889 and 1890, English hoop makers, with a duty of 35 per cent. agamst them, exported about half the quantity of cotton ties .required for their cotton crop. This year, with cotton ties duty free, they are beaten by the ArACtiCall manufacturer at least 103. per ton. Whether the necessity has arisen for the local iron- worker to do his beet, we must leave them to judge and decide for themselves. Under any circumstances, we cannot see any prosoect of an increased demand for their labour; but with mutual confidence and readiness to adapt themselves to the new conditions, we believe we may hold our own to our mutual benefit, and the wel- fare of the town and neighbourhood.—Yours truly, F. MONKS.

div.head: NEWTON ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE NEWTON ELECTIONS.

Sir.—A correspondence begun in your paper has been dragsed out of your columns into a contemporary but as many of your readers are interested in the subjects under review I beg of you the favour of a little space at the same time.a.s "Elector " asked me to reply to him and all the other aliases,l do so now merely to say that I am quite at a loss to understand why these writers have imported so much rancour and bitterness into their writ- ing. lam sorry to say I cannot compliment any of them upon their style of controversy,nor will it advance the cause of truth and justice. Moreover, it seems to me that the matters in debate are practically conceded: for in the report of the Connsel's meeting held on the sth of the month it is stated the Commissioners' opin- ion on the question of talking tells on the Common was referred back to the sub-committee, which, I assume, is adverse to the Commissioners' claim. And, in the second place. " El.ctor," after consulta- tion, now says, !. When none of the trustees are elected by the people, or nominated by the Council, the Council may appoint additional trustees, but only so many as the Charity Commissioners think fit." We have had good representation, so far, and unless " ElPctor's " soaring ambition would like to add only one mere I think we shall be sutficiently represented in the two gentle- men who have every likelihood of being returned at the head of the poll in the Viaduct Ward and in the Crow- lane ward. I must confess,before We part compan y,that I am disappointed with" Elector" whose behaviour is more like that of Ehud, both fair and false for while professing friendliness in his first letter he stabs me under the belt in his second in that awkward left handed manner of his : and (as in that case) "the dirt came out." I reproduce his letter of the 15th October, in which he says " In the past I believe you, Mr. Campbell have ever endeavoured to be on the side of justice; do not desert it now,but come forward and give us a help- ing hand in this, our time of need. I should he delighted to see you in the field as A candidate, and I know there are o:-hers of the same opinion ;" and in his last letter he says, in conclusion, " I detest the man who stands like a cur to he kicked by every worshipper of Vicuna who has a sixpence more than he in his pocket, and confound the men who stand idly by, while wrong is being done, say I." This gentleman, though neither lawyer nor grammar- ian, yet commits himself to an opinion in this fashion. " The qnestion of a lease does not affect the subject at

issue ;" and says that " it is immaterial to the rate- payers whether Mr. Waterworth has a lease or not." Indeed! But suppose the lord of the manor should step in and ask the Commissioners why they prevent his tenant fulfilling the conditions of his lease what would become of " Elector's " £1,400? In a word I think "Elector "a very unsafe guide in law and logic. Be, however, refers me to "Looker-on," who should have taken the cognomen of "putter-on," and he would ex- actly play the part as described by Antigonus in " A Winter's Tale." This gentleman says : " What ! to hunt with the hounds and run with the hare ?" and evi- dently doesn't like the idea thrown out by " Elector " who invites me to enter the field as a candidate, oblivious of the fact that the law has thrown down the barriers which such gentry are industriously trying to build up against the common people again. This person draws my attention to the actions of certain people, Congregational ministers, miner's agents and others. But my experience of Congregationul ministers is that they are not so easily nose-led as he would have us sup- pose. I have also the honour to be acquainted with all the miner's leaders in this part of the country, and in particular with Mr. Sam Woods, M.P., who is a wonder- fully shrewd man of his day and generation, and would on no account "follow a multitude to do evil." If I thought this" Looker-on" could appreciate Shakespeare I would tell him in the words of Iago— " Good name, in man and woman dear, my lord, Is the immediate jewel of their souls. Who steals my purse, steals trash, 'tis something, nothing: 'T was mine 'tis his, and has been slave to thousands ; But he who filches from me my good name, Robs me of that which not enriches him, a And makes me poor indeed."

And while doing so desire the printer to be very particu- lar with the technical part of the quotation which is often made into "pie." As I have much respect for the "Law," if not for lawyers, I can only observe that as of old this one is "willing to justify himself" for giving any opinion at all, but then it is considered chic to have a cut if only to keep his small wit from dying out, I am glad he did not indulge in any dog-latin, "and so on." " Artisan " was so good as to pay me a cempliment, for which I thank him, and to suggest that I might know something else that was worth making copy of. No doubt my friend, no doubt, but we will reserve all that for som other occasion when your minds are more at ease and you can listen calmly and without reviling the gods. This has all been by way of diverting public attention from the real question at issue, which is—Shall we or shall we not have the same men or class of men to administer our affairs. I attended one ward meeting though not by special request—in fact I believe there was some notice to the effect that only those belonging to that ward were desired. Well, I thoaght while some of the candidates were speaking (one cannot always revel a thought) the others "deserved to he locked up," ahem, they followed each other with such dreary mono- tony, but to my unspeakable relief, one cf them waxed righteously indignant at the very thought that he knew nothing of the accounts of the Dean School Trust being great at accounts. The gentleman who preceded him gave his word of honour that the accounts were all right. as right as a trivet. This little comedy gave rise to the following reflection: First, why these gentlemen had so persistently kept from the public the accounts showing the actual cost of the New Town Hall of which not a penny piece is as yet paid off, and why the annual accounts are so mixed up that no one but an expert can tell how our finances stand—whether we are gradually getting deeper into debt or getting out of debt. I could put a whole string of questions on this subject which I am quite sure "Elector" and all the other small fry would leave severely alone, wrapping themselves up in their dignity. There would be no rushing into the breach to oppose the supposed foe. I do not for a moment say the questions formulated were not of imminence but I say they are not of the first, or, if you like the last importance. Many were of importance and will cost much money so that the next Council will not be by any means an economical one if some of the candidates get in. Most fortunately not above one half of them can get in. Well then who are most likely to get in? The answer is simplicity it- self. Thatside which is most largely represented whether Whig or Tory, church or chapel. So far we have as far as is known the following cana idates In Newton ward: 4 Conservatives, 2 Liberals. In Crow-lane ward: 5 Conservatives, 1 Liberal. In Town Hall ward : 3 Conservatives, 3 Liberals. In Viaduct ward : 4 Liberals. In Wargrave ward: 4 Conservatives, 2 Liberals. Conservatives 16, Liberals 12. Of these, 5 are Churchmen and 1 Dissent in Newton ward.

4 are Churchmen and 2 Dissent in Crow-lane ward. 3 are Churchmen and 3 Dissent in Town Hall ward. 1 Churchman and 3 Dissent in Viaduct ward. 5 are Churchmen and 1 Dissent in War grave ward. Churchmen 18, Dissentors 10. Rumour has it that there are other two, one on each side both of politics and religion. In the Newton ward the 3 nominated by the Ward Committee areboth Church and Tory. The other three run independently, 2 being I church and 1 chapel, and of these one is Liberal one Conservative and one unknown on politics. The Chnrch and Tory ticket will be issued in a week or so we sup- pose. The Liberal has issued his, and the Conservative his preliminary and the third is in reserve. In Crow- lane, the rory is the tick.t. This wa, supposed to be the only debateable ward but the Tory is going to have a practical walk-over unless the Liberal gird up his loins and prepare a man tor the struggle. Their best man dropped out without rhyme or reason leaving five Toriei and one Liberal. In the 'Town Hall ward the tisket is Liberal, the other two or three, "as the case may he " are Tory of whom two are also on one ticket, leaving a " strag " but as good a man as any. In the Viaduct ward, Liberal is the ticket with a very slight variety, but as only three man can get in the fourth is the unknown quantity. In the Wargrave ward Tory and Church is the ticket, the red flag being also torn to ribbons. As a matter of speculation we will suppose the Tories to gain the first two places in the following wards : Newton, Crow-lane and Wargrave and the Liberals the first two in Viaduct and Town Hall, this would give the Tory element a longer lease of electoral power than the Liberals to start with and with the blood set spinning through their sluggish system perhaps rouse them to reorganize their forces. The men who get in as Liberals should have remembered that the fire and force that carried them into power and office needed to be fed both with the oil of sympathy and by putting their odd sixpenny pieces together against a time of political need.—l am yours as ever, P. M. CAMPBELL.

Sir,—Our attention has been drawn to the report in your issue of the 10th inst., of the firo at the Millstone Inn. You say " A supply of water was obtained from Messrs. Gillespie and Mason's paper mill opposite, but the building was prac'ically gutted bofore the fire was extinguished." The facts are just the opposite of this. But for the timely assistance of our men and hose the place would have been completely gutted. Our hose was put on very expeditiously, and almost at once- ex- tinzuished the flames, and we think that the least the Insurance Company could have done would be to acknowledge the services rendered, by a correct re- port of the matter.—We are, yours. Szl.. GILLESPIE AND MASON, LIMITED, RICHARD BARTON, Director. Newton Paper Mills, 15th November, 1894. •
HALTON.

MEETING OF THE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.—The minutes of the last meeting of the Balton Parochial Committee, held on the 10th inst. in the Wesleyan Schoolroom under the presidency of the Rev. G. D. Wray, were submitted at the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sani- tary Authority on Tuesday for confirmation.—They showed that the Clerk had reported to the Committee that in accordance with their instructions he had written to Dr. Adams, the medical officer to the Authority, for a more explicit statement as to what ought to be done at Elalton Brook in order to comply with the provisions of the Rivers Pollution Prevention Ad.,. To this the medical officer had replied saying that he would like to meet the Committee on the ground. The Committee then decided to accede to this request, and that the In- spector of Nuisances also be asked to be present on the ground on the date fixed when he would be expected to he prepared to finish his report to the Committee with respect to Bate's Bridge.—On the motion of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Knowles, the minutes were adopted. LECTURE ON "PARISH COTINCILS."—A lecture was delivered on this subject by Mr. Joseph Pritchard, of Runcorn, on Friday evening in the Girls' Schoolroom, Halton. There was a large attendance of ratepayers and the chair was occupied by the Rev. G. D. Wray vicar of Balton. In the course of his remarks Mr. Prit- chard said that there were few measures which had been passed by any legislative assenihly which were likely td have a more permanent effect upon the social well tieing, happiness, and prosperity of country life than the Parish Councils Act. The measure had been truly called the Magna Charta of the 19::h Century, for if carried out in a proper spirit it would indeed prove a charter of liberty for the People of the rural districts. (Applause.) Votes of thanks closed the meeting.

div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.

It does not often happen that whea two teams engage with each other in a game of Rugby football that they retire from the contest with the score standing just as they started. But such was the case at Widnes on Saturday when Warrington met the men of chemicals. The Lowerhouss ground was the scene of operations, a field, which, by the way, is situated far from the chemical fumes and almost unapproachable in muddy weather. The Warrington and Widnes match is always a sufficient attraction to draw a big crowd to witness the game, and Saturday proved no exception to the rule.

The Widnesians were confident of victory and they were not reluctant to express it. Furthermore, it was not to be denied that they had strong grounds f)r so thinking. Widnes have this season done remarkably well, carrying everything before them, and they now occupy premier position in the Second League Champion- ship. They have only been defeated once thus far this season, and that was at the hands of Wigan by a try to nil. Only three points have been scored against them in all the other matches put together, and these three points were scored by Barrow, at Barrow, the second in the League. The previous four matches on the Lower house ground with Warrington had also ehded favour- ably for Widnes, and their supporters were sanguine' enough to believe that the wirepullers were beaten before they entered the field. On the other hand the Warring- ton team was far from being one to be over-confident in, as five of the "A " team men were again drafted into the team. But to give honour where honour is due it must be admitted that the five substitutes acquitted themselves admirably.

The game itself was a most interesting and evenly- contested one. The only drawback was the heavy downpour of rain which occurred during the progress of the match. The wet grass made running very difficult, and the greasy state of the ball caused accurate passing to be almost impossible. During the first half of the game Warrington had the disadvantage of playing against the wind, but the teams were so evenly matched that throughout neither side scored. Again and again was the citadel of each team invaded in turn, but on each occasion was the defence equal to the attack. If any disadvantage could be claimed between the two , rivals it appeared to rest with Warrington who on one or two occasions experienced the hardest of luck in not scoring. Warrington played a more open game than usual, and thus gave the backs a better opportunity of showing their ability.

Boscow again maintained his reputation of " surefoot " at full back and on his present form Warrington may be considered to have one of the best full backs in the county. Moores' first performance at three-quarters in the first team was favourably commented upon, and Burton played as fine a game as he has done this season. Foden and Bate worked well together at half back, but the forwards were weaker than usual, Jolley, who was doing duty for Lancashire county against Westmoreland, being one of the absentees.

It was pleasant to see that the eld rivalry which has existed so long between the teams did not carry the players beyond bounds as has previously been the case, and it is to be hoped that the same will hold good when the return match is played. The long line of victories which has followed the track of the Widnes players seems to have had a beneficial effect upon the Widnes spectators as they were a trifle less biassed in their judg- ments than on previous occasions when the wirepollers have been their visitors. A little incident occurred just as the spectators were wending their way home along the muddy roads. A Warrington 'bus condwctor as he flitted past with his 'bus load of passengers for Warring- ton seemed to enjoy teasing the Widnesians by shouting "Well you have given Warrington a beating."

I notice that on Saturday in the match between Run corn and Swinton. Barber, who played with Warrington last year, and who has been a member of the Stockton Heath team thus far this season, was playing three- quarters for the dark greens. He also distinguished himself by scoring a very clever try. Barber has with- out doubt a bright future before him in football circles, but would it not be better for him to play for his own

town? The clubs in the first division of the League are be- coming beautifully less. First Leigh were suspended and relegated to the bottom place. Then Salford were expunged from it, and now Wigan have received their quietus until February Ist. A great sensation was caused when Leigh were suspended, but suspensions are now becoming so common, that they only excite a platonic interest. Not a single club which has been "tried "has been acquitted,so that it looks serious for the remaining four clubs whose turn has yet to come. On Tuesday next Tyldesley have to face the committee, and it is not unlikely that they will suffer a like fate to their neigh- bours at Leigh. It is a singular fact that despite the disarrangement of fixtures caused by these susnensions, Warrington have not yet had to look out for fresh ones, as the Wigan fixture is not due until March.

By the way, an injustice is being done to the clubs remaining in the competition by thes. suspensions. The suspended clubs are struck out of the competition, and yet the points which various clubs have scored against them are allowed to remain. For instance, if the points which Oldham,Tvldesley,and Wigan have scored against Salford were expunged from the table as they ought to be,. Warrington, who have not met Salford would now head the League. It is to be hoped that this matter will be attended to, as the competition will be of no value if tho clubs do not play an equal number of matches. From present appearances,however, it would appear that Warrington will have a walk over for the cup by being the only club left in.

Warrington have a very good fixture to-day. The Tranrnere fixture has been cancelled, and Halifax, the Yorkshire Cup holders have been taken on instead. This team which contains a number of international players should prove a great attraction, as they are noted for playing a very open game, and have some very speedy backs. To cope with them, the following team has been chosen by Warrington :—full back, Boscow ; three quarters, Cunninham ; Fleesom, Burton, Moores; half- backs, Bate and Foden ; forwards, Turner, Thorniley, Dakin, Berry, Taylor, Andrews, Savage, and Bailey.

A very good match was witnessed by an equally good " zate " at Liverpool-road on Saturday, between St. Mary's, the Warrington junior cup holders. and Pember- ton -Recs, the Wigan junior cup holdets. The two teams had previously met at Pemberton when the result was a draw. The " Marys " however gained a substantial victory on Saturday. They have yet to be beaten either at home or away, and it would be difficult to find a better junior team tor miles round. They have a good lot of players all round.

The Lancashire County Committee have shown their- appreciation of Jolley's play by choosing, him for every match in which Lancashire has takm part in this season: He is down to play Cumberland at Fallowfield to-da.y,and he has, probably with the exception of Valentine taken part in more county matches than any other in the team, for he has played regularly for Lancashire for several years. On SaturJay, after Hurst was hurt, in the match with Westmoreland, Jolley was taken out of the forwards tc play three-quartemand I hear he played very well in this position. Dakin„of Warrington, has been on the reserve for Lancashire on several occasions, but he has not yet played his first county match. He is again on the reserve against Cumberland, and Ii hope that this time, he will be given a chance.

The hopes of Lancashire of regaining' ths county championship were very hricht up to last week, but with such capable men as Varlev and Hurst haviim their collar bones brol:en, that prospect has been sli2htly clouded. Good substitutes have been found, however, in Lees of Oldham, and Floltres of Morecambe, and these two men will be tested sufficiently in the match with Cumberland this afternoon.

TEMPERANCE SERVICE OP SONG.

A temperance service of song, entitled "Harry Beckwith," was rendered in excellent styde by the Independent Methodist choir, of Crossley-st., on Saturday evening, in aid of the funds of the Tem- perance Hall. Mr. W. Barton was in charge of the musical arrangements,. and Mr. James Shaw read the connective readings. The 'Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis) presided, and stated that he was pleased to see workingmen manifesting such a deep interest in the great temperance movement. Many great and able men were now taking up the work of temperance refprni. Mr. Chamberlain, who was a great politician, and the Bishop of Chester among ether bishops were mentioned. During the service, the choir received many rounds of well-merited ap- plause from the large audience. Mr. R. Storey pro- posed, and Mr. S. Drury seconded, a hearty vota of thanks to the Rector for hiskind, genial andrahle services in the chair. The meeting responded with long and loud applause. Mr.J. Righy,in pro-oosing a vote of thanks to the choir. spoke highly of the manner in which the service of song had been gone through. Mr. S. Stringer seconded, and tha resolu- tion was put to the meeting by the Rector-and car- ried. Pen the Rector pronounced the Benediction and dismissed the gathering. On Sunday evening, a Gospel temperance meeting was held in) the above hall. Mr. J. Drury presided. Sr.wiNG MACHINES, Hand £2 13s. 6d. Treadle £4 4s. with handsome walnut cover.—J. and W. DUTTigf, 16 and 13, Sankey-at., Warrington.— A drot. BOLD-STREET CHAPEL.—SERVICE Sz FOR THE PEOPLE.

There was a large attendance 0 the service at Bold-street on Sunday. afternoon. The short act- dress, hearty singing, efficient solos, and excellent performances of the orchestral hand, all combine to make the services increasingly popular. At the commencement of the ineeting-,, the and played "In the Chapel," by R. Eilenbarg„ Mr. Edgar tam- ford gave a violoncello solo, which received well- merited applause. The Rev. J.. Kirtlan, who occu- pied the chair, then referred to the prominence of music in the Sunday afternoon services. They had all derived great pleasure from it, and it was impos- sible to say too much in its praise. believed that the time was coming when the music would constitute even a greater portion of the worship of GO than at the present time. Mr. J. Horton was then called upon to give an address. HA said that while the character of nations was influenced by great men, there was some sphere in which every- one, however insignificant, had an influence either for good or for evil. It was their duty not only to

avoid that which was wrong,but also to strive after that which was good and noble and pure: Let them all endeavour to leavß the world better than they found it. div.head: )BECTURIC ON "JOHN HOWARD, THE PRE3ON PHILANTHROPIST.:.
div.p: )BECTURIC ON "JOHN HOWARD, THE PRE3ON PHILANTHROPIST.:.

A lecture was given by the Rev. S. T:-Wardle Stafford of Torlroon Monday evening at the litm-sey- road Wesleyan Chapel, upon the above subject. The chair was occupied by Mr. E. Richardson, and there was a very good audience. Previous to. the lecture, Mr.. IC Wadsworth, the organisto gave an excellent organ. recital, which was listened to, with great interest.

, The • Chairman briefly addressed the meeting, and then called 'upon Mr. Stafford to proceed with hisdecture The lecturer in the course of his address said that John Howard was the pioneer of modern philanthropy, and it was for the encouragement of young,men who were present thathe had chosen that subject for his address that night. Howard was certainly no, genius,but was essentially a common-place man. He wan, born in or near London in 1727. His ancestors dictnot seem to have been sufficiently remarkable to have anything par- ticulartold of them. His mother died when he was a child: His father had the reputation of. being," stingy,' and if•this were so, it is a remarkablecireumetanee that he should be the father of the man whesegenerosity was unbounded. The elder Howard; hovvevere was an upright, Christian man, and his influence was great over his son. The subject of the lecture was sent to school at anearly age, and he was very consistent in one res- pect, and that was keeping at the bottom.ol; the class. Of his attainments at school a friend of Howard had said that of the rules of grammar he knew nothing, of languages, ancient and modern, ditto, end his own lan- guage he could never speak grammatically: When he was twelve years of 'age he was apprenticKite. a groce-, and thus his father put a trade into his fingers, In 1742; his apprenticeship terminated by the death of his father, who left him £7,doGo 4 together with considerable preperte. A \ clause was put in the will that he was not to come, into possession until he was 24 years of age, but such was the opinion of his integrity entertained by the executors that they allowed him to come into it at. once: Mr. Stafford., sketched in eloquent terms,, the various . points of inter— est in Howard's career. He said that he, was a most kind and considerate landlord, and hezompletely trans- formed the village of Cardington, in yehich he lived, From being a centre of vice, it became.a model villages. tm 1773, he became. Sheriff of Bedfordshire, and while- he held this office„, he became enoet active in prison Worm, travelling. the lengt4 and ,breadth of Eng,iandi cellecting evidence•to show the aborninabre state in which the prisoners were, kept. The result of these visits was that two bills were passed through Parliament to ameli- orate their condition. Howard wee.. arse called tee-the bar of the House, and ordered to receive the thanks, ol ,Parliament for his exertions in favour of prison reform - In addition to his work in 3ugland4he travelled ulLovey Europe visiting the various prisons and hoTitals, was during a tour of this kind this he fell ill at. Pusan in the Crimea in, 1690. The illness was soon found,tc.be fatal, and on January 21. e 1700,the,passeci away .to the higher service of the skies at the. age of 64 years. In the Parish Church at Cardingtone a marble tabletwas placed to his memory with the inscriptioa.." 2ohn Howard, died' at Cusany „Russian Tartars-, Jenualy 21, 1790, aged %years. Cleriat is cur hope." The-If:fel of Howard was an example of ,what an unedecatel man could do. He (the lecturer).. wished everyenet .) take courage and be inspired by. Howard's life. _dere. was a man who did a leree amount of-good, and yet he could not spell a word of mere than, two syllabics., ilis life was an incentive and encouragement to everyone to do what he could for, the.. amelioration cZe his fellow creatures..

A hearty rote of thanks raw accorded to the• Lecturer and Chairman on the inotion,c>f Mr. Daveyrfieoonded by the Rev:. Gwen WatizinF, ,and the rneetic4.., ()hosed with the pronouncing of the benediction.

COUNTY OF CHESTER, RABIES ORDER OF 1892. -- MUZZLING OF DOGS. --- NOTICE IS HriiEVY G 1 at at a Meeting of the Executive Committee of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, under the Diseases of Animals Acts, 1894, held at Chester Castle, on Thursday, the Bth day of November, 1894, IT WAS ORDERED that with the exception of the following Townships, viz : Dukinfield Disley Hattersley Etchells-in-Northern Hollingworth Etchells-in-Stockport Matley Handforth Mottram-in-Longdendale Marple Tintwistle Norbury Werneth Northen Bosden Offerton Bramhall Romiley Bredbury Torkington Brinnington Yeardsley-cum-Whaley Cheadle embracing that portion of the County under the juris- diction of the said executive Committee, known as the Hyde and Stockport Police Divisions, the exemptions set out in the Special Regulations as to Dogs made by the said Executive Committee on the 9th day of Decem- ber,lB92 be extended to Dogs which have on a Collar with the name and address of the Owner of the Dog legibly engraved thereon, the effect of which Order is that DOGS in any portion of the County under the jurisdiction of the said Executive Committee with the exception of such portion of the said district as is em- braced within the Townships herein mentioned NEED NOT BE MUZZLED provided they have on a Collar as herein mentioned but subject as aforesaid the said Re- gulations of the 9th day of Desember.lB92, will continue to remain in operation until further modified or re- voked. REGINALD POTTS. Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Chester, 9th of November, 1894. The District of the Local Authority of the County of Chester does not include the City of Chester, nor any of the Municipal Boroughs, either wholly or partly within this County,

COUNTY OF CHESTER. pISEASES OF ANIMALS ACT, 1894. SWINE FEVER. MOVEMENT OF SWINE FROM IRELAND. NOTICE is Hereby Given, that at a Meeting of the Executive Committee of the Local Authority of the County of Chester under the above Act, held at Chester Castle on Thursday, the Bth day ot Nov., 1894, IT WAS ORDERED that from and after Monday, the welith day of November, 1894, until the Thirtieth day ot November, 1894, both days inclusive, the MOVE- MENT OF SWINE into the District of the Local Autho- rity of this County from IRELAND shall be and hereby is ABSOLUTELY PROHIBITED.
